Chapter 1 Introduction

Communication is central to human connection; it enables individuals to interact, build relationships, and participate in society. People communicate through five primary and often overlapping modalities: verbal speech, non-verbal cues, written text, visual representations, and active listening [25]. While these modes enable effective interaction for much of the global population, they are not equally accessible to everyone. For an estimated 430 million people worldwide who are deaf or hard-of-hearing [29], sign languages serve as a primary means of communication, offering rich linguistic structures expressed through body movement and facial expression [28, 10].

Over the past decade, human–computer interaction (HCI) has been reshaped by machine learning and computer vision, shifting from purely keyboard-and-mouse input toward more natural modalities such as vision-guided, voice-enabled, and gesture-based interaction. In assistive technology, sign language recognition systems now achieve high accuracy using RGB1 cameras, depth sensors, and wearable IMU/EMG devices, translating sequences of signs into text or speech and thereby mediating communication between deaf and hearing users [39, 20, 18, 36, 38, 13]. Yet, these systems still face persistent challenges in robustness “in the wild,” signer and domain generalization, and coverage across diverse sign languages, limiting their deployment beyond controlled settings [39, 9, 7].

In parallel, a line of work has focused on representing sign languages in machine-readable form. Early descriptive and markup languages—such as HamNoSys and its XML2-based derivative SiGML3, as well as related avatar-driven systems like eSIGN and SignSynth—encode handshape, location, movement, and non-manual markers for synthesis by virtual humans [3, 2, 12, 15]. These frameworks, along with corpus-driven pipelines that map glosses to pose sequences and then to rendered video [26, 9, 11] have been crucial in standardizing how signs are described and animated. However, user studies consistently show that current pose-based and GAN4-based generation still struggle with fast hand motion, co-articulation, and facial grammar, yielding synthetic videos that are only partially intelligible to fluent signers [9, 35]. Recent end-to-end and gloss-free sign language production models—such as Cross-Modal Contrastive Creator (CCC) and multilingual generators like Signs as Tokens—demonstrate impressive progress, but they also underline ongoing difficulties in semantic–motion alignment, naturalness, and scalability [42, 44, 17, 43].

1.1 Background

Early sign language technologies, such as fingerspelling-to-text systems, have demonstrated promise but typically target narrow sub-tasks. For example, smartwatch-based systems that take advantage of Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensors have proven to recognise ASL5 alphabet sequences or short sentences from wrist motion alone, and EMG-based approaches classify a limited set of handshapes or isolated signs with high accuracy [14]. These systems are valuable proofs of concept, but they do not deliver the end-to-end text-to-sign capabilities that DuoSign aims to provide.

Beyond fingerspelling, prior work has explored a spectrum of sensing and synthesis strategies. Wearable devices based on IMUs, EMG, or hybrid armbands have been used for continuous ASL and CSL recognition and even end-to-end sign-to-speech translation [14, 39]. Vision-based systems such as OpenPose and MediaPipe leverage pose estimation to recognise full-body Korean Sign Language (KSL) or Chinese Sign Language (CSL) motion from RGB video and have taken a leap further in detecting non-manual signals like facial expression to boost accuracy [6, 30, 9].

On the generation side, in the early and mid-2000s, avatar animation pipelines such as eSIGN and WebSign were developed to show realistic signing avatars that were structured & linguistically informed representations that made use of markup language (e.g., SML6, SiGML) [22, 3]. More recent gloss-based pipelines and neural sign-generation models extend this idea by composing skeleton sequences from lexicons and rendering them with neural or rule-based avatars [26, 35].

While African nations host diverse Deaf communities with rich sign language traditions, including Ghanaian Sign Language (GhSL), Kenyan Sign Language (KeSL), Nigerian Sign Language (NSL), and many others, these languages remain severely underrepresented in assistive technology research. The primary barrier is data scarcity: unlike German Sign Language (DGS) Corpus, as utilized in Amit Moryossef’s "An Open-Source Gloss-Based Baseline for Spoken to Signed Language Translation", which benefits from decades of corpus development, large-scale datasets, and government and institutional support, African Sign Languages lack the extensive annotated video corpora, lexical databases, and motion-capture resources needed to train modern neural generation systems. This creates a cycle in which data scarcity impedes tool development [37], because reproducing comparable corpora, annotation pipelines, and signer datasets requires substantial funding, and this further marginalises hard-of-hearing people in these communities [9, 24, 4].

DuoSign is designed to sit precisely in this gap by providing a modular, web-based, openly available English-to-ASL generation pipeline that others can inspect, extend, and benchmark against, without rebuilding the entire stack from scratch.

1.2 Problem Definition & Context

Despite rapid advances in sign-language technology, the overwhelming majority of research targets the recognition direction—converting signs into text for hearing users. The reverse direction, generating sign language from text, remains significantly underexplored in academic literature. Recent surveys of sign-language processing highlight that most benchmark efforts and public datasets concentrate on sign-to-text translation, leaving text-to-sign pipelines scarcely explored [44]. This imbalance creates a communicative asymmetry: deaf individuals can express themselves through systems that interpret their signs, yet the replies they receive are rendered only as plain written language, which is not their primary linguistic modality.

This asymmetry has a tangible human cost. Deaf individuals are frequently excluded from spontaneous, informal communication—not just formal settings—because the tools designed to support inclusive communication have not addressed the generation side of the problem. Receiving a response in plain English, when a person’s first language is sign language—which can take many forms such as American (ASL), British (BSL), or Ghanaian (GhSL)—is linguistically and culturally reductive. Sign languages are not simplified versions of spoken languages; they have distinct grammar, spatial structure, and non-manual markers that carry grammatical meaning [26]. Stripping all of that from a response produces something functional but incomplete.

1.2.1 Directionality Gap: Who Gets Served?

Recognition has been the dominant direction in sign language technology. Surveys and system overviews foreground pipelines that detect and classify signed input—using vision-based hand tracking, glove sensors, or wearable IMU/EMG devices [25]. The same orientation appears in wearable sensor work. DeepSLR uses two armbands with IMU and multi-channel sEMG to recognize continuous Chinese Sign Language sentences and convert them into speech in real time. SignSpeaker deploys a smartwatch to recognize American Sign Language sentences and output spoken English through a paired smartphone, achieving a word error rate of around 1% on its sentence set. Other systems use smartwatches and consumer wearables to detect ASL letters or short words from wrist motion, or EMG bands to classify a fixed set of ASL hand motions and alphabet letters with high accuracy. Across these projects, the information flow is overwhelmingly from sign-to-text or sign-to-speech: they are designed to help hearing people understand signed input. This directionality gap is central to DuoSign’s motivation.

Recent efforts have begun to address the generation gap. Moryossef et al.’s open-source baseline demonstrates reproducible text-to-gloss-to-pose translation for Swiss German, Swiss French, and Swiss Italian sign languages [26], and the research.sign.mt platform provides accessible resources and tools for sign language processing. These contributions represent meaningful progress toward democratizing sign language technology.

Despite this rich ecosystem, a stark asymmetry persists: most deployed systems focus on recognition (sign-to-text) rather than generation (text-to-sign). Even state-of-the-art generators are often closed-source, difficult to reproduce, and rarely tailored to African local sign languages [26, 35].

From a user perspective, this directionality has concrete implications. In many real-world interactions—a deaf student reading course materials online, a deaf professional navigating a web-based HR7 system, or a deaf person accessing a digital government service—the available tools make it easier to convert signing into written or spoken language than to present information back to the user in their primary signed language.

1.2.2 Intelligibility-Replicability Tradeoff

The second problem concerns how existing generation approaches trade off intelligibility, naturalness, and replicability—especially in lower-resource settings.

Early avatar systems such as eSIGN rely on linguistic notation and rule-based synthesis. Authors describe signs using HamNoSys and SiGML, encoding handshape, location, palm orientation, and movement, and a sign-language editing environment then composes these elements into avatar motion [15]. This representation is compact and language-agnostic at the notation level, and it supports flexible rendering within the manually authored domain. However, creating and maintaining a large lexicon in HamNoSys requires specialist expertise; extending coverage to new domains or sign languages is labour-intensive; and generating smooth co-articulation between consecutive signs is non-trivial. The eSIGN project explicitly restricts itself to limited, pre-scripted content and notes that fully automatic translation from arbitrary text into sign is not feasible with their approach.

Corpus-driven pipelines move generation closer to real signing. How2Sign introduces an 80-hour multimodal ASL corpus with RGB, depth, 2D keypoints for more than six million frames, and a 3D pose subset recorded in the CMU8 Panoptic Studio [9]. Duarte et al. use these modalities to train pose-estimation and GAN-based video synthesis models, then evaluate whether ASL users can understand the resulting synthetic signing. Their user study is instructive: while participants can often identify the broad topic of a synthetic video, the skeleton overlays and GAN-generated clips are only partially intelligible at the sentence level, with fast hand motion, co-articulation, and facial grammar cited as major sources of confusion. They conclude that current pose- and GAN-based generation does not yet support fully reliable comprehension for fluent signers.

Recent neural text-to-sign models such as CCC and Signs as Tokens underscore both the promise and the limitations of fully learned generation [42, 44]. Both papers highlight ongoing challenges: semantic-motion alignment remains fragile; high-quality generation depends on large, carefully curated corpora; and extending the approach to new sign languages is constrained by the availability and quality of 3D motion annotations.

Taken together, these works reveal a consistent “ceiling.” Notation-driven avatars are linguistically explicit and relatively light-weight, but they require expensive lexicon building and are often perceived as stiff or robotic by fluent signers. Pose- and GAN-based systems grounded in real signing can achieve more natural motion, but current models still produce only partially intelligible output and are tightly coupled to large, language-specific corpora. Even where code is released, pipelines are deeply entwined with particular datasets, transcription conventions, and avatars, making them difficult to reproduce or adapt for lower-resource sign languages.

1.3 Objectives and Significance

In addressing the communication barriers faced by deaf and hard-of-hearing users, the goal is to design and build a system with the following aims:

  1. Develop functionality that supports accessible, sign-first communication in common digital contexts.
  2. Implement an algorithm that translates English text into American Sign Language (ASL) gloss.
  3. Design friendly VRM avatars that perform sign language using natural, expressive motion.
  4. Prototype a lightweight browser-based reader-assistant workflow that captures text from webpages (including user-highlighted passages, pasted text, and available video captions such as YouTube subtitles) and renders sign-language output through a signing avatar or skeleton.
1.3.1 Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals

This project aligns with three United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):

  • SDG 4 (Quality Education): About 80% of deaf individuals worldwide face educational barriers due to limited access to sign-language resources [29]. DuoSign reduces this gap by enabling on-demand translation of learning materials into ASL. A deaf student in Ghana or Philadelphia can access textbook content in their primary language without relying on interpreter availability.
  • SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities): Hearing users often benefit from speech recognition and translation tools in their native modalities, while deaf users are commonly expected to rely on written text. DuoSign helps close this asymmetry by prioritizing text-to-sign translation rather than placing the adaptation burden on deaf users.
  • SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth): Many workplace exclusions for deaf professionals stem from communication barriers rather than capability gaps. A browser-based tool that translates workplace emails, policies, and documentation into sign language makes inclusive employment more practical, even for organizations with limited technical budgets.

1.4 Review of Literature and Related Works

This literature review covers the foundations most relevant to DuoSign: the history of sign language technology, sign language linguistics, glosses as an intermediate representation, skeletal-pose modelling, low-resource data constraints, and related work in sign recognition and generation.

1.4.1 History of Sign Language Technology

Sign language technology has historically prioritized recognition over generation, leaving a major access gap for deaf users. Early systems in the 1980s focused on notation-driven avatars—formal systems like HamNoSys that broke signs into handshapes, locations, and movements, then tried to “play them back” through animated characters. Projects like eSIGN (2002–2008) demonstrated that this could technically work for narrow domains (government e-services in BSL, DGS, and NGT)9, but the avatars looked robotic, required specialist linguistic expertise to author content, and couldn’t automatically translate arbitrary text into signing[15]. The 2010s brought motion capture approaches, where researchers recorded real signers with optical tracking to drive avatars. These looked more natural—co-articulation and timing came for free—but building even a 1,000-sign lexicon required months of studio time and tens of thousands of dollars[8]. The 2018–present era introduced neural generation pipelines: text-to-gloss-to-pose-to-video systems trained on parallel corpora like RWTH-PHOENIX-Weather10 and How2Sign [35, 9]. These systems hit decent automatic metrics (BLEU11 0.6) but struggled with comprehension—user studies showed deaf signers could identify topics but not full sentences, citing missing facial grammar and choppy motion[9]. The common thread: recognition (sign-to-text) has always gotten more attention than generation (text-to-sign), leaving deaf users with tools that help hearing people understand them but do not help them consume information in their primary language.

1.4.2 Sign Language Linguistics: Why This Is Harder Than It Looks

Sign languages are not manual versions of spoken languages. Contrary to a common but misguided belief, ASL is not “English on the hands”; it has its own grammar, spatial syntax, and phonological system realized through handshape, location, movement, palm orientation, and non-manual markers such as facial expressions, head position, and eyebrow configuration [31]. Three things make this computationally difficult.

First, simultaneity: spoken-language phonemes happen sequentially (one sound after another), but sign-language parameters happen at the same time—a sign like MOTHER in ASL combines a “5” handshape, chin location, tapping movement, and neutral facial expression all at once. Most NLP models, including transformers, are built for sequences and struggle with this [4].

Second, spatial syntax: sign languages use 3D signing space to encode grammatical relations—verbs inflect for subject and object by changing start/end locations, pronouns are realized by pointing to where referents were established earlier in the discourse (for example, signing “I” means pointing to the speaker), and entire clauses can be spatially indexed. Text-to-gloss translation cannot fully capture this because glosses are linear [26].

Third, non-manual markers (NMMs): raised eyebrows mark yes/no questions, furrowed brows mark wh-questions (information-seeking questions such as who, what, where, when, why, and how), and headshakes mark negation. These are not just emotional expressions—they are grammatical. Most sign-language datasets do not annotate NMMs at the frame level, so current generation systems either omit them or copy them blindly from source videos without checking whether they match sentence structure [21].

1.4.3 Glosses: Necessary Evil or Fundamental Limitation?

Most papers have argued against the use of glosses, questioning their effectiveness and appropriateness for generating sign-language videos. However, the core issue is that glosses are lossy. Glosses are word-level labels for signs, written in capital letters (e.g., MOTHER, GO, WHERE). They serve as an intermediate representation in many sign-language systems because they are easier to work with than raw video: you can train a neural machine-translation model to map English text to ASL glosses, then look up each gloss in a dictionary to retrieve a pose sequence. The problem is that glosses are lossy. They do not encode spatial syntax (which hand location corresponds to which discourse referent), non-manual markers (is this a question or a statement?), or classifier constructions (how multiple objects are arranged in space) [26]. Linguists have also pointed out that glossing conventions vary across research groups, making datasets harder to combine and reducing inter-annotator consistency [26]. Recent work has tried to bypass glosses entirely—models like CCC and Signs as Tokens learn direct text-to-pose mappings using discrete motion tokenization [42, 44]—but they still struggle with semantic alignment: how do you map abstract concepts like “obligation” or “conditionality” to specific signing patterns when your training data only provides noisy sentence-level supervision? For now, glosses remain pragmatically useful but linguistically incomplete, and DuoSign uses them as a stepping stone while acknowledging their limitations.

1.4.4 Skeletal Poses as Representation

Skeletal pose sequences—2D or 3D coordinates of body joints over time—have become the de facto representation for sign language in computer vision. Tools like OpenPose and MediaPipe extract pose keypoints from RGB video in real time, providing a structured, lower-dimensional input for recognition and generation models [9]. For recognition, pose-based approaches often outperform raw-pixel models because they discard irrelevant background information and focus on body configuration, and they are computationally lighter to process. They primarily use temporal body-joint coordinates rather than full image tensors. For generation, pose sequences serve as the “skeleton” that drives avatar animation—either by directly manipulating a 3D humanoid model (inverse kinematics) or by conditioning a GAN to synthesize photorealistic video from skeletal input [35]. The catch is that pose estimation degrades in the wild: hands become unreliable during fast motion or occlusion, facial landmarks are coarse and miss subtle mouth morphemes, and 2D projections lose depth information needed to distinguish signs like THINK (hand at forehead) vs. KNOW (hand at temple) [9]. The How2Sign dataset addressed this by recording signers with depth cameras and motion capture for a subset of data, but that level of infrastructure is not available for most sign languages and is difficult to reproduce for most systems. DuoSign uses MediaPipe Tasks (formerly MediaPipe Holistic) for pose extraction because it is free, runs in the browser, and works on standard webcam footage—trading off some precision for accessibility.

1.4.5 Data Scarcity and the Low-Resource Challenge

For many African sign languages, the volume of available data is unknown as much as it is scarce. Part of this traces back to the diversity of African spoken languages—and sign languages follow the same fault lines. Just as spoken languages across the continent diverge in vocabulary and grammar, so do their signed counterparts. The sign language situation in West Africa alone has been described as “as diverse as it is undocumented” [26].

This creates a structural cycle rather than a single isolated problem. Low documentation and fragmented standards make corpus creation difficult; without corpora, tool development remains slow and expensive; without usable tools, deaf communities stay digitally marginalized; and that marginalization weakens the institutional and funding support needed to build new datasets.

Figure 1.1 visualizes this cycle and marks DuoSign’s intended intervention point.

This problem is reinforced by linguistic fragmentation. A sign in one language can mean something entirely different in another, and the literature describes these as “false friends”—signs that share form but diverge in meaning across sign languages [26]. A gesture that means lonely in ASL, for instance, is routinely misread as “be quiet” because it visually resembles a common hushing gesture [26]. The same dynamic applies across national sign languages: a sign in BSL may carry a different or even opposite meaning in Korean Sign Language, not because either community made an error, but because each language evolved independently within its own cultural context. This makes dataset transfer and model reuse harder, which increases the cost of building new resources from scratch.

The problem is also structurally uneven across regions. In Europe and a few betterresourced contexts, a small set of language, e.g. German Sign Language (DGS), benefit from large annotated corpora, detailed gloss transcriptions, and institutional backing. The RWTH-PHOENIX-Weather dataset (8,257 DGS sentences from weather broadcasts) and How2Sign (80+ hours of ASL instructional videos) represent years of coordinated effort involving linguists, native signers, and motion capture studios [26, 9]. Meanwhile, most of the world’s 200–300 sign languages have no computational datasets at all, including virtually all African, South Asian, and Southeast Asian sign languages.

Ghanaian Sign Language (GhSL), used by roughly 10,000 deaf Ghanaians—though community estimates place the broader deaf population at around 500,000—has no publicly available corpus, no standardized glossing conventions, and minimal documentation beyond print dictionaries [29]. The same is true for Kenyan Sign Language (KeSL), Nigerian Sign Language (NSL), and dozens of others. Building a corpus requires institutional partnerships with Deaf community organizations, trained linguists, native signers willing to be recorded, ethical review protocols, and long-term maintenance infrastructure. In low-resource settings, these prerequisites are difficult to assemble at once, so the absence of data persists and downstream tool development remains stalled.

Taken together, these barriers limit tool development, reinforce digital marginalization, and suppress the institutional support needed for new data collection. DuoSign does not solve those structural constraints on its own—it cannot create African sign language corpora out of thin air—but it targets a practical leverage point: lowering implementation cost when data does become available. By providing a reproducible, modular pipeline, African researchers can adapt an existing system instead of rebuilding the full stack from scratch.

1.4.6 Related Works: Recognition vs. Generation
1.4.6.1 Recognition Systems: The Dominant Direction

Most sign language research still targets recognition (sign-to-text), not generation (text-to-sign). Vision-based systems use RGB cameras and pose estimation (OpenPose, MediaPipe) to recognize isolated signs or continuous sentences [25]. Wearable systems use IMU sensors and EMG armbands to classify signs from wrist motion and muscle activity. For example, SignSpeaker on a smartwatch reports 99% accuracy on continuous ASL sentences, and a Myo-based setup distinguishes 80 ASL signs at 96% accuracy [18, 14]. These systems help hearing users understand signers, but they do little to help deaf users consume information in their primary language. This recognition-first pattern is partly driven by funding priorities (speech technology has a clearer commercial market), easier evaluation (word error rate is straightforward), and a persistent assumption that spoken language is the “default.” For many deaf users, however, the urgent direction is text-to-sign: reading textbooks, navigating workplace portals, or accessing online video content without full caption support.

1.4.6.2 Generation Systems: Four Decades of Avatars

Text-to-sign generation has evolved across roughly three phases. In the notation-driven era (1980s–2010), systems like HamNoSys encoded signs as symbolic parameters and animated avatars by “playing back” those symbols. The eSIGN project used this model for government e-services in BSL, DGS, and NGT, but outputs often looked robotic, required specialist authoring expertise, and did not generalize to arbitrary text input [15]. In the motion-capture phase (2010–2018), researchers recorded real signers with optical tracking to drive 3D models, which improved naturalness but made lexicon growth expensive and slow (even a 1,000-sign lexicon could take months) [8]. The current neural phase (2018–present) uses text-to-gloss-to-pose-to-video pipelines trained on corpora such as RWTH-PHOENIX and How2Sign [35, 9]. These systems can report reasonable BLEU scores (around 0.6), yet user studies still show limited sentence-level comprehension, often due to weak facial grammar and uneven motion quality [9]. More recent gloss-free approaches (CCC, Signs as Tokens) learn motion codes directly from text and improve some automatic metrics, but non-manual markers remain a persistent gap [42, 44]. In short, technical performance has improved, but linguistic completeness remains the harder problem.

1.4.6.3 Where DuoSign Fits

DuoSign occupies a middle ground between research-grade prototypes and practically deployable accessibility tools. It is designed as a browser-based, openly inspectable baseline that prioritises sign generation, accessibility, and reproducibility over benchmark-driven complexity.

Most importantly, whereas systems such as SignSpeaker primarily optimise recognition, DuoSign prioritises the reverse direction: presenting information back to deaf users in a signed modality rather than only translating their input for hearing audiences.

The current system has clear limitations: it does not yet provide full grammatical facial-expression modelling, it has limited support for complex two-handed spatial constructions, and it inherits vocabulary constraints from the 2,000-word-class WLASL corpus (11,980 video clips in the processed subset). Even so, DuoSign is intentionally designed as a modular and reproducible plug-and-play baseline for African deployment contexts where motion-capture infrastructure and large curated corpora are often unavailable. The long-term objective is not to outperform data-intensive benchmark models, but to provide a practical foundation that can be incrementally localised—most importantly toward Ghanaian Sign Language (GhSL)—by researchers and community developers without rebuilding the entire stack.

1.4.6.4 Analysis of Related Works

A comparative matrix of representative sign-language systems is provided in Appendix D (Table 4). The key pattern is consistent: highly natural systems typically require expensive data or compute, while easily deployable systems tend to compromise naturalness or linguistic coverage. DuoSign is positioned as a reproducible middle ground focused on text-to-sign generation for practical deployment.

Key Observations

  • Directionality gap: Recognition systems still dominate deployment, while generation systems remain less common and less accessible.
  • Infrastructure tradeoff: The most natural outputs generally come from motion capture or GPU-heavy pipelines, which are hard to reproduce in low-resource settings.
  • Replicability constraint: Open implementations are increasing, but many are tightly coupled to specific corpora and annotation schemes.
  • DuoSign’s position: DuoSign prioritizes reproducibility and portability, accepting moderate quality constraints to enable practical text-to-sign access on consumer hardware.

Chapter 2 Requirements

This chapter focuses on the stakeholder identification, requirements gathering, and analysis phase of DuoSign. It examines what target users need, how they expect to interact with the system, and where existing sign language technologies still fall short. Using use-case analysis, the chapter establishes the foundation for a system architecture and design that address these needs and support the project’s accessibility goals.

2.1 Requirements Elicitation

Sommerville [34] identifies three main techniques for requirements elicitation: talking to stakeholders directly, observing existing systems in use, and reading existing documents and literature. For DuoSign, the third approach was used, drawing on published research, dataset documentation, and established accessibility standards.

2.1.1 Literature Review

Requirements were gathered by reviewing prior work on text-to-sign language generation. We examined eSIGN [15], Text2Sign [35], and Sign.MT [26]1 to identify what already works, where current systems fall short, and which user needs remain unmet. Four gaps stood out: many systems relied on synthetic or notation-driven animation instead of real video; no single system combined voice input, video export, and browser-based rendering; and existing systems were not designed for an African deployment context: they depend on large language-specific corpora, stable high-bandwidth infrastructure, and compute resources that are often unavailable in low-resource settings. These gaps directly informed what DuoSign set out to implement.

2.1.2 Secondary Data from Existing User Studies

No direct interviews with deaf users were conducted for this project. Instead, user requirements were derived from published studies and dataset documentation. The WLASL dataset [23] includes recordings from real deaf signers, so its signs reflect real usage. ASL-LEX [33]2 documents how signs are used in everyday ASL and informed the synonym lookup strategy in the gloss lexicon. In both datasets, the deaf community contributed to the source research. This project therefore builds on that input indirectly.

2.1.3 Accessibility Standards

Non-functional accessibility requirements came from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG3) 2.1 Level AA4, which specifies colour contrast ratios, minimum touch target sizes, and keyboard navigability. These guidelines represent decades of research into what disabled users actually need. Applying them to the interface directly meant there was no need to rediscover those requirements from scratch through fresh user testing.

2.1.4 Limitations and Future Evaluation

The main limitation of this approach is the lack of direct consultation with deaf or hard-of-hearing users. No interviews, surveys, or usability tests were run. As a result, some choices, such as the default avatar, preferred playback speed, and level of visual detail, are based on literature-backed assumptions rather than direct user testing. A dedicated usability study with deaf participants is the next step.

2.2 Key Stakeholders

DuoSign is engineered to target a broad and diverse user base spanning deaf communities, educational institutions, and the research ecosystem. Among the many potential stakeholders, the following groups were identified as key informants for requirements elicitation:

  • Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Individuals: The primary beneficiaries of the system. They need access to written content rendered in their primary visual language rather than plain text. DuoSign allows them to receive information in ASL rather than having to adapt to English grammar for every interaction. For authenticated users, the ability to export signed animations as downloadable MP4 videos further enables offline access and sharing of translated content.
  • Hearing Individuals and Content Creators: People who interact with deaf individuals and want to communicate in a more linguistically respectful form than plain text, without requiring sign language training. This group also includes content creators, such as educators, social media producers, and accessibility officers, who want to produce signed video directly from written material without commissioning separate interpreter recordings.
  • ASL Learners and Students: People learning ASL who need an interactive, on-demand tool for understanding how English maps to ASL grammar. Mainstream language platforms support many spoken languages, but equivalent large-scale support for ASL is still limited. DuoSign addresses this with gloss token breakdowns, skeleton visualisation, and adjustable playback speed so learners can study signs at their own pace.
  • Public Institutions and Accessibility Offices: Schools, hospitals, universities, and government offices that need scalable tools for making public-facing written content accessible to deaf communities without relying entirely on the availability of human interpreters. The system’s REST5 API and video export capability enable institutions to integrate sign language generation into existing workflows programmatically.
  • Researchers and Developers: Researchers who need a reproducible, open baseline to benchmark new translation approaches against, and developers who need an API for adding sign language output to existing applications without building the full pipeline themselves. DuoSign exposes RESTful endpoints for translation, pose data retrieval, audio transcription, and vocabulary lookup, enabling programmatic integration and downstream experimentation.

2.3 Use Case Analysis

Use-case diagrams model the behaviour of a system and help to understand and capture its requirements. They describe the high-level functions and scope of a system and illustrate how actors interact with the system rather than how the system operates internally [19]. DuoSign’s components are modelled with a single use-case diagram to provide an overview of how actors use and interact with the system. See Figure 2.1.

2.3.1 End-Users

The system’s end-users are the individuals who directly interact with and use the system regularly. The user roles and their interactions are as follows:

Guest User

  • Input English text (up to 500 characters) and receive a corresponding ASL avatar animation.
  • Use voice input via microphone as an alternative to typed text, with clear visual feedback indicating listening, idle, and error states.
  • Guest users may translate up to five words or gloss tokens before being prompted to log in or create an account.
  • View real-time sign rendering with the gloss token breakdown displayed alongside the avatar.
  • Switch between display modes (3D avatar, skeleton overlay, or hidden) to examine pose data at different levels of abstraction.
  • Select from multiple avatar models and choose between close-up, full-body, and 3D world view modes.
  • Control playback with pause, resume, previous/next token navigation, replay, and adjustable speed (0.5×, 1×, 1.5×, 2×).
  • Access the system from any modern browser without installing additional software or creating an account, subject to a configurable per-session translation limit.
  • Guest users cannot export MP4 videos and cannot access translation history actions (search, filter, replay from history, re-edit, or delete saved entries).

Authenticated User

  • All capabilities available to Guest Users, without a translation limit.
  • Export any translation, whether current or from history, as a downloadable MP4 video of the avatar performing the sign sequence.
  • Create an account and log in to unlock persistent access once the guest usage threshold is reached, without blocking translation during the registration prompt.
  • View previously translated phrases in a searchable, filterable translation history, grouped by date and annotated with input type (typed, voiced).
  • Replay, re-edit, or delete any saved history entry.

Content Creator

  • Translate written English content into ASL avatar animations directly from the web application.
  • Export signed animations as MP4 video files for embedding in presentations, social media posts, instructional materials, or websites, without commissioning professional interpreter video production.
  • Customise avatar appearance and view mode to produce output that fits the visual style of their content.
  • Verify accessibility of written content by checking its signed rendering before publication.

ASL Learner

  • View gloss token breakdowns alongside avatar animations to understand the English-to-ASL grammatical mapping sign by sign.
  • Switch to skeleton visualisation mode to observe raw pose landmarks without avatar rendering, aiding understanding of body and hand positioning.
  • Replay saved translations at reduced speed (0.5×) to study individual signs in detail.
  • Navigate token-by-token through a signed sequence using previous and next controls to isolate specific signs.
  • Build a personal study library using the translation history, returning to previously translated phrases for repeated practice.
2.3.2 System Workflows

The use-case diagram establishes what actors can do, while activity diagrams show how those interactions unfold in practice. Activity diagrams capture the full workflow lifecycle, including decision points, parallel paths, and failure branches, at a level of detail that use cases alone do not provide [19]. The three activity diagrams below model DuoSign’s principal workflows: core translation and playback, video export, and history management.

2.3.2.1 Core Translation Workflow

Figure 2.2 models the end-to-end translation flow from the moment a user provides input to the point at which the avatar animation completes and the result is persisted to history.6 The diagram covers both typed and voice input paths, the two-phase streaming response in which the rule-based result is emitted immediately followed by an optional LLM quality-improvement event, the three-way animation source resolution order (WLASL video, pose binary, or fingerspelling fallback), and the configurable guest usage threshold that triggers a non-blocking registration prompt without interrupting the translation in progress.

2.3.2.2 Video Export Workflow

Figure 2.3 models the export pipeline available to authenticated users. A browser-compatibility fork determines the capture mode: real-time WebM recording via the MediaRecorder API on supported browsers, or a JPEG7 frame-array fallback for environments such as Safari that do not implement the MediaRecorder interface. Both paths converge at the backend, where FFmpeg encodes the captured data into a downloadable H.264 MP4 file at 1280×720 resolution.

2.3.2.3 History and Replay Workflow

Figure 2.4 models the lifecycle of a translation history entry from creation to deletion.8Entries are appended to browser-local storage on every successful translation, subject to a 100-entry FIFO eviction policy. The diagram also shows the four actions an authenticated user may perform on any saved entry: replay, export, re-edit, and delete. The replay mechanism uses URL9 parameters to open the translation page with pre-filled text and autoplay enabled. This keeps the history and translation pages linked without requiring shared server-side session state.

2.3.3 Behavioural Model

Activity diagrams model workflows across actors, while state machine diagrams model the lifecycle of a single system object. Harel’s statechart formalism [16], standardised in UML10 2.5.1, fits event-driven components with explicit transition guards, which matches the behaviour of a media playback controller. Figure 2.5 models the DuoSign avatar animation player, including its four states (Idle, Playing, Paused, Complete), the guard conditions for each transition, and the speed multiplier that sets per-token delay.11

2.4 System Requirements

The 1990 IEEE12 Standard Glossary of Software Engineering Terminology defines a requirement as (1) a condition or capability needed by a user to solve a problem or achieve an objective; (2) a condition or capability that must be met or possessed by a system or system component to satisfy a contract, standard, specification, or other formally imposed document; and (3) a documented representation of a condition or capability as in (1) or (2) [1]. From our engagement with stakeholders and analysis of the problem space, we gathered requirements that were meticulously ranked by order of priority for implementation.

2.4.1 Functional Requirements

[FR001] – The system shall accept English text input of up to 500 characters and produce a corresponding ASL avatar animation.

[FR002] – The system shall support voice input via two complementary paths: browser-based speech recognition using the Web Speech API for real-time transcription, and server-side transcription using the Groq Whisper API for uploaded audio files, supporting WebM, MP3, WAV, M4A, OGG, and MP4 formats up to 25 MB13.

[FR003] – The system shall convert English text into ASL gloss notation using a spaCy-based rule pipeline that handles pronoun substitution, time-fronting, subject-object-verb reordering, and negation-final constructs, with an LLM fallback for edge cases the rule pipeline cannot resolve.

[FR004] – The system shall expose translation results through a streaming Server-Sent Events (SSE) endpoint that emits an immediate rule-based result, followed by an optional LLM refinement event, so the frontend can update results progressively without blocking the user.

[FR005] – The system shall render sign animations using a VRM-format 3D avatar driven by pose data extracted from real WLASL sign language videos via MediaPipe Tasks and mapped to bone rotations using Kalidokit.

[FR006] – The system shall fall back to fingerspelling for any word not found in the gloss lexicon or its synonyms by expanding the word character by character, ensuring all input text produces a visual output.

[FR007] – The system shall display real-time gloss token breakdowns alongside the avatar animation to show the English-to-ASL grammatical mapping at the word level.

[FR008] – The system shall provide playback controls for the sign animation sequence, including play, pause, replay, previous token, next token, and a cyclic speed selector with 0.5×, 1×, 1.5×, and 2× playback rates.

[FR009] – The system shall support multiple avatar display modes: 3D VRM avatar and skeleton pose overlay.

[FR010] – The system shall support multiple camera view modes (close-up interpreter, full body, and 3D world), switchable at any time during playback.

[FR011] – The system shall offer multiple VRM avatar models and allow users to switch between avatar appearances without interrupting the sign sequence.

[FR012] – The system shall let authenticated users record the animated avatar canvas and export the sign sequence as a downloadable MP4 file, using MediaRecorder with WebM output where supported and a JPEG frame-array fallback for incompatible browsers, followed by server-side FFmpeg conversion to H.264 MP4.

[FR013] – The system shall allow users to create accounts and log in after reaching a configurable guest usage threshold, without blocking the translation in progress during the registration prompt.

[FR014] – Registered users shall be able to view, search, filter, replay, export, re-edit, and delete previously translated phrases from a persistent translation history grouped by date and filterable by input type and date range; guest users shall not have access to these history-management actions.

[FR015] – The system shall track guest usage through a session-based browser identifier and prompt registration at a configurable threshold without interrupting the translation in progress.

[FR016] – The backend shall expose RESTful API endpoints for translation (rule-based, streaming, and audio), gloss lexicon lookup and search, pose and video-file serving, video export conversion, and health checks.

[FR017] – The system shall normalise pose landmarks extracted from WLASL videos to correct for inconsistent signer framing across the dataset.

2.4.2 Non-Functional Requirements

[NFR001] – Usability: All core actions shall be reachable within two steps from the main screen. During playback, the word currently being signed shall be highlighted so users can follow along without losing their place. The system shall keep users informed of what is happening at every stage, including during long-running operations such as video export.

[NFR002] – Responsiveness: The system shall return an initial translation result within 300 milliseconds under normal network conditions. The avatar animation shall begin within one second of the translation being received. The user shall not be blocked or prevented from interacting with the system while a background quality-improvement step is running. Video downloads shall be ready within a time proportional to the length of the signed sequence.

[NFR003] – Accessibility: The interface shall follow established web accessibility guidelines, including sufficient colour contrast, adequately sized touch targets for mobile use, full keyboard navigation, and a readable text summary of the signed output for users who cannot view the animation. The avatar display shall include an option to show only the skeletal pose, and an option to hide the animation entirely so users who only need the text output are not forced to load rendering components.

[NFR004] – Voice Input Feedback: The microphone feature shall clearly communicate to the user whether it is actively listening, waiting, or has encountered a problem, so users always know what the microphone is doing.

[NFR005] – Performance: The system shall handle multiple simultaneous users without a noticeable drop in translation speed. The avatar animation shall play back smoothly without stuttering or frame drops. Exported videos shall be produced at a quality suitable for sharing or embedding in other materials.

[NFR006] – Security: User account passwords shall be stored in a secure, irreversible form. Login sessions shall be managed using tokens that cannot be read or modified by browser scripts or third-party page content. The system shall enforce limits on how frequently any single user can make requests, to protect against misuse. Audio and image data submitted for processing shall be discarded by the server as soon as the request is complete.

[NFR007] – Scalability: Each major component of the system (the translation engine, animation renderer, and sign vocabulary) shall be replaceable independently without requiring changes to the rest of the system. The server-side API shall act as the single point of integration for future client surfaces, such as a mobile application or browser extension.

[NFR008] – Maintainability: The server-side code shall separate concerns into distinct layers so that changes to one layer do not require changes to the others. The client-side code shall be organised by feature so that individual parts of the interface can be modified without affecting unrelated parts.

[NFR009] – Reliability: The system shall always produce a visual output for any input text, even when the exact sign is not in the vocabulary. If the primary translation pathway fails, the system shall automatically attempt a simpler fallback before showing an error to the user. If the preferred animation source for a sign is unavailable, the system shall try alternative sources before spelling the word out letter by letter.

[NFR010] – Deployability: All components of the system shall be deployable using free hosting plans so that the project can be demonstrated without incurring any infrastructure costs.

[NFR011] – Browser Compatibility: The system shall work correctly on all major modern web browsers. Any feature that is not supported in a particular browser shall have a working alternative, so that no user loses access to core functionality based on their choice of browser.

[NFR012] – Portability: The system shall run entirely within the user’s web browser. No software installation, browser plugin, or device-specific hardware shall be required to access any feature of the system.

[NFR013] – Learnability: A first-time user shall be able to perform a complete translation and view the resulting animation without reading any documentation or on-screen instructions.

[NFR014] – Error Recoverability: When any part of the system encounters a problem, it shall display a plain, non-technical message and give the user a clear way to try again, without requiring a full page reload or loss of previously entered text.

[NFR015] – Transparency: The system shall never present a translation as a black box. The sequence of sign tokens derived from the input shall always be shown alongside the animation so users can read, understand, and verify what the avatar is signing.

[NFR016] – Offline Resilience: The core translation feature shall continue to function if external AI14 services are temporarily unavailable, by falling back to the built-in rule-based translation pathway without displaying an error to the user.

[NFR017] – Privacy by Design: The system shall collect only the minimum data required for its operation. No user input, audio, or image data shall be stored on the server after the corresponding request has been completed.

[NFR018] – Extensibility: The system architecture shall not make assumptions specific to American Sign Language. The sign vocabulary, translation rules, and avatar motion data shall each be replaceable to support future adaptation to other sign languages, including Ghanaian Sign Language.

[NFR019] – Content Authenticity: All avatar animations shall be derived from recordings of real human signers. The system shall not use computer-generated or fabricated sign motions in place of recordings from real signers.

[NFR020] – Cultural Appropriateness: The default avatar shall suit the cultural context of the users this system was built for. Users shall be able to choose from avatars with different skin tones and clothing styles so that people from different backgrounds can find one that feels like them.

2.4.5 Acceptance Criteria for Critical Requirements

The following measurable acceptance criteria are used to verify the most critical requirements.

  • AC1 (FR001): Given English input of 500 characters or fewer, the system returns a non-empty gloss sequence and starts avatar playback.
  • AC2 (FR002): A user can trigger translation through either live microphone input or uploaded audio, and both paths produce transcribed text sent to the translation pipeline.
  • AC3 (FR004): For streaming translation, the frontend receives an initial rule-based event before any optional LLM refinement event.
  • AC4 (FR006): When a token is missing from the glossary and synonym set, the system outputs a fingerspelled sequence instead of an empty result.
  • AC5 (FR008): Playback controls allow pause/resume, replay, previous/next token navigation, and speed switching across 0.5×, 1×, 1.5×, and 2×.
  • AC6 (FR012): An authenticated user can export a played sequence and download an H.264 MP4 file for that sequence.
  • AC7 (FR014): An authenticated user can search, filter, replay, re-edit, export, and delete saved history items; guest users cannot access these actions.
  • AC8 (NFR002): Avatar playback begins within one second after translation output is received by the client.
  • AC9 (NFR006): Passwords are never stored in plain text, authenticated sessions use protected tokens, and request rate limits are enforced at the API boundary.
  • AC10 (NFR009): For any valid user input, the system either signs a known token or falls back to an alternative path (synonym/fingerspelling), preventing empty visual output.

2.5 DuoSign: Proposed System

From the system requirements gathered, the proposed system is a browser-based text-to-sign pipeline that accepts typed or spoken English, converts it to ASL gloss, and presents the result through an animated avatar. The detailed architectural rationale, technology choices, and deployment design are discussed in Chapter 3 (Section 3.1).

At the requirements stage, the key point is not the individual framework choices but the system shape: DuoSign separates language processing, animation, and media delivery so that each part can evolve independently. This modularity supports maintainability, extensibility, and future localisation to other signed languages while keeping the user-facing workflow simple. An extended comparison with representative prior systems is provided in Appendix C (Table 3).

2.6 Ethics

The design and implementation of DuoSign raise several ethical considerations that have been carefully addressed throughout the project:

Data Privacy. User data should not be retained beyond the immediate request scope unless the user has explicitly chosen to store it. Privacy is therefore treated as a design principle that constrains system behaviour rather than as a purely technical afterthought.

Responsible Use of Sign Language Datasets. The WLASL dataset [23] was used in accordance with its licence and citation requirements. The dataset is acknowledged as belonging to the linguistic community that produced it, and its use in this project respects the intellectual contribution of deaf signers and sign language researchers.

Avoiding Misrepresentation. The system uses real sign language videos as the source for avatar animation rather than synthetically generated motion, grounding output in authentic signing. Limitations in gloss accuracy and non-manual marker representation are documented transparently rather than concealed. The system does not claim to produce grammatically perfect ASL output, and the displayed gloss token breakdown makes the translation’s intermediate representation visible to the user rather than presenting output as a black box.

Not Replacing Human Interpreters. DuoSign is designed as a supplementary accessibility tool for contexts where no interpreter is available. It is not a replacement for qualified sign language professionals in critical settings such as healthcare or legal proceedings. This distinction is made explicit in the system’s documentation and user interface.

Cultural Sensitivity. The system does not imply that ASL is interchangeable with Ghanaian Sign Language or other regional sign languages. The modular architecture is designed to support future localisation into GhSL as a documented future work direction, acknowledging the linguistic distinctiveness of each sign language.
