Chapter 3 Architecture and Design

This chapter presents the architecture and design of DuoSign, the English-to-American Sign Language (ASL) translation system built for this project. It describes the structure of the software, the major components, how they connect, and the reasoning behind each decision. Every choice made here traces back to a functional or non-functional requirement established in Chapter 2.

3.1 System Architecture

DuoSign is built around a modular pipeline architecture that breaks the system into independently deployable services, each responsible for a single domain: natural language processing, pose extraction, avatar animation, or user interface rendering. Services communicate only through documented REST endpoints or file-based exchanges, with no shared internal state across boundaries.

This structure fits DuoSign for concrete reasons. The translation process is sequential: English text becomes ASL gloss notation, gloss tokens map to animation data, and animation data drives the avatar. Moryossef et al. describe this text-to-gloss-to-pose-to-video flow as the standard decomposition for spoken-to-signed language systems [26], and DuoSign follows that structure. Beyond ordering, the system spans human-computer interaction, computational linguistics, computer vision, and real-time 3D graphics. Separating the Python NLP backend from the JavaScript rendering engine lets each side use tools suited to its own workload. A researcher who wants to replace the rule-based NLP module with a neural model only needs to match the API contract, and the avatar pipeline remains unchanged. This directly supports NFR007 (scalability) and NFR018 (extensibility).

One core design decision in DuoSign is splitting compute-heavy media work from linguistic processing. Natural language processing and audio transcription run server-side on FastAPI, where Python’s NLP stack is strongest. Video decoding, pose landmark extraction, and avatar rendering run client-side in the browser, where MediaPipe WebAssembly1 and Three.js WebGL2 use the user’s hardware directly. This avoids streaming raw video between client and server, reduces latency, and keeps backend load low.

3.1.1 Frontend Architecture
3.1.1.1 Feature-Sliced Design (FSD)

The frontend uses Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), which organizes code by domain responsibility rather than technical role. Instead of placing all React components in one folder and all hooks in another, FSD defines five layers: app, entities, features, widgets, and shared. Each layer can import only from lower layers. This rule prevents circular dependencies by design and makes feature-level changes safer and easier [40].

FSD was selected over a conventional components/hooks/pages layout for three DuoSign-specific reasons. First, the application spans distinct domains, including avatar animation, voice input, translation history, and NLP integration. Each domain is kept in its own features/ slice with separate model/ and ui/ folders, so one feature can evolve without destabilizing others. Second, the widget layer assembles AvatarPanel, InputPanel, and NavigationBar into stable page-level blocks that routes can consume directly. Third, this dependency structure maps cleanly to Next.js 14 App Router, where route files stay thin and focus on composition. This structure supports FR001 (translation interface), FR009 (history view), and FR013 (settings view).

3.1.2 Backend Architecture
3.1.2.1 FastAPI NLP and Export Service

The backend is a Python FastAPI service with three core responsibilities: text-to-gloss NLP processing, server-side audio transcription through the Groq Whisper API, and video export encoding through FFmpeg. FastAPI was chosen over Flask and Django for its native async/await concurrency model, automatic OpenAPI3 documentation, and direct fit browsers. 2WebGL = Web Graphics Library, a browser API for hardware-accelerated 2D/3D rendering. 3OpenAPI = A standard specification format for describing REST APIs. with Python NLP tooling. The service exposes focused endpoints: POST /api/translate, POST /api/translate/fast, POST /api/translate/stream (SSE4), POST /api/translate/audi

GET /api/vocabulary, GET /api/pose/{gloss}, GET /api/video/{gloss}, POST

/api/export/video, and GET /api/health. This backend/frontend boundary supports FR003 (text-to-gloss), FR002 (voice transcription), and FR012 (video export).

3.1.3 Detailed Architecture Using the C4 Model

This chapter uses the C45 model to present DuoSign’s architecture. C4 is an abstraction-first approach that reflects how engineers reason about real systems [5]. It defines four levels of detail: Context (Level 1), Containers (Level 2), Components (Level 3), and Code (Level 4). DuoSign uses the first three levels, which are sufficient to communicate architecture and design decisions without dropping to line-level implementation.

3.1.3.1 System Context Diagram (Level 1)

The system context diagram is the starting point. At this highest level, DuoSign is shown as one system with its external actors and connected services. Figure 3.1 shows these relationships.

  • Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing User: Represents end users whose primary language is ASL. These users submit English text (typed or pasted) and receive sign language animations rendered by a 3D avatar, enabling them to consume written content in their preferred visual language.
  • Hearing User: Represents hearing individuals who interact with deaf colleagues, students, or community members. These users type responses into DuoSign and receive signed avatar output, allowing them to communicate in a linguistically respectful form without requiring sign language training.
  • ASL Learner: Represents students and self-directed learners studying American Sign Language. These users type English sentences and receive both the ASL gloss breakdown and the corresponding avatar animation, providing immediate visual feedback on how English grammar maps to ASL structure.
  • Content Creator: Represents educators, accessibility officers, and social media producers who use DuoSign’s video export feature to generate signed MP4 content from written text, without requiring professional interpreter video production.
  • Developer and Researcher: Represents technical users who interact with DuoSign programmatically. These users call the translation API directly, swap the NLP module for their own models following the documented API contract, extend the lexicon with new sign data, and benchmark translation quality against the rule-based baseline.
  • DuoSign: Represents the core software system under consideration, responsible for converting English text into ASL gloss notation, mapping gloss tokens to pose animation data, rendering sign language animations through a 3D avatar in real time, recording and exporting signed video, and serving media assets on demand.
  • Web Speech API (Browser-native): External browser-native speech recognition system used by DuoSign’s primary voice input path. Transcription occurs entirely within the browser without transmitting audio to any server; the browser returns a text string that is fed directly into the translation pipeline.
  • Groq API (Server-side): External AI inference platform hosting the whisper-large-v3-turbo model used for DuoSign’s secondary voice input path. The FastAPI backend forwards raw audio blobs received from the client to this service for transcription and discards the audio after the resulting text is returned. This path is used when the Web Speech API is unavailable or when higher multilingual accuracy is required.
  • Groq LLM (Translation Fallback): External LLM inference endpoint used as the text-to-gloss fallback when the rule-based NLP pipeline produces a confidence score below the configured threshold. Invoked only for complex or idiomatic sentences that the spaCy-based pipeline cannot handle adequately.
  • FFmpeg (Bundled via imageio-ffmpeg): Video encoding library used to convert canvas-captured WebM recordings or JPEG frame arrays into H.2646 MP4 files. Bundled with the FastAPI backend via the imageio-ffmpeg package, which includes a self-contained FFmpeg binary requiring no system-level installation.
  • Supabase (Storage and Database): External managed platform used for both storage and database services. Supabase Storage hosts sign language reference videos, precomputed pose files, and avatar models as publicly accessible objects delivered over CDN; the frontend fetches them directly over HTTPS. Supabase PostgreSQL stores user accounts, session tokens, and server-side translation history.
3.1.3.2 Container Diagram (Level 2)

Next is the container diagram, which zooms into DuoSign and shows the high-level technical building blocks. In the C4 model, a container is a separately runnable or deployable unit that executes code or stores data. See Figure 3.2. This diagram shows each container as a box with its internal details abstracted away. The containers are:

  • Next.js Frontend (Web Application): A React-based web application built with Next.js that serves as the primary user-facing interface. It handles text input, dual-path voice input, avatar rendering using Three.js and the VRM format, client-side pose playback via .pose file parsing, video-driven landmarking via MediaPipe Tasks Vision (WebAssembly), canvas recording and MP4 export, and translation history management via localStorage. Next.js is chosen over plain React for its server-side rendering capabilities and native WebAssembly support, both required for running MediaPipe in the browser. The frontend communicates with the backend through HTTPS REST calls and fetches media assets directly from the asset bucket.
  • FastAPI Backend (API Application): A Python-based API application responsible for text-to-gloss NLP processing, voice transcription, vocabulary serving, media asset delivery, and video export conversion. It employs FastAPI for its native async support, automatic OpenAPI documentation, and Python’s NLP ecosystem. The backend reads gloss data from glosses.tsv, delegates audio to the Groq Whisper API, and invokes FFmpeg for MP4 conversion. In the current prototype, sign media assets are served directly from a local bucket/ directory; in deployment, asset requests are proxied to Supabase Storage.
  • Supabase Storage (Media Asset Store): An S3-compatible object store hosting sign language reference videos (.mp4), precomputed pose landmark files (.pose), and VRM avatar model files. In the current prototype, this is a local bucket/ directory. In production, Supabase Storage is used: it provides 100 GB of free storage, a built-in global CDN, and a public URL per asset, without requiring a separate storage platform alongside the database.
  • Supabase PostgreSQL (Relational Database): A managed PostgreSQL instance hosted on Supabase that stores user accounts, session tokens, guest usage counters, and translation history for registered users.
3.1.3.3 Component Diagram (Level 3)

Finally, each container is further decomposed to identify and show the internal components and how they interact with each other. See Figures 3.3 and 3.4.

Next.js Frontend Components. The frontend container is decomposed into the following components, organised by FSD layer:

  • TranslatePage / HistoryPage / SettingsPage (App Layer): Thin Next.js App Router page files that orchestrate widget composition without containing business logic. Each addresses a corresponding section of requirements: TranslatePage satisfies FR001, FR002, FR007–FR011; HistoryPage satisfies FR014; SettingsPage addresses avatar and preference customisation.
  • AvatarPanel / InputPanel / NavigationBar (Widget Layer): Composite UI blocks that assemble feature slices into page-level sections. AvatarPanel integrates the VRM canvas, playback controls, avatar switcher, view mode selector, skeleton toggle, and export button into one cohesive surface.
  • useTranslate (Feature: translate-text): The primary translation hook. Calls POST /api/translate/stream for SSE-streamed progressive results, falling back to POST /api/translate/fast if streaming fails. Handles IX-marker substitution (IX-1 → I, IX-2 → YOU), abort control for cancellation, and debug metadata (method, confidence, processing time). Satisfies FR003, FR004.
  • useVideoEngine (Feature: animate-avatar): The primary animation driver in the default avatar render mode. Fetches sign videos from Supabase Storage CDN, plays each through a hidden <video> element, pipes decoded frames through MediaPipe Tasks Vision (HolisticLandmarker running as WebAssembly), and drives the VRM rig via Kalidokit. When no source video is found for a gloss token, delegates to usePosePlayer as the fallback. Satisfies FR005, FR008.
  • usePosePlayer (Feature: animate-avatar): Animation driver for the skeleton render mode and the pose-based fallback path. Fetches .pose binary files from GET /api/pose/{gloss}, parses the precomputed landmark frames in JavaScript, and drives the VRM rig via Kalidokit frame by frame. Maintains an in-memory Map cache keyed by gloss name to avoid refetching. Falls back to fingerspelling for unknown glosses. Also serves as the fallback called by useVideoEngine when a source video cannot be retrieved. Satisfies FR005, FR008.
  • useCanvasRecorder (Feature: animate-avatar): Manages canvas-to-MP4 recording. Selects between the captureStream/MediaRecorder path (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) and a JPEG frame-sampling path (Safari/iOS), uploads the result to POST /api/export/video, and triggers a file download. Satisfies FR012.
  • ExportVideoModal (Feature: animate-avatar): React component managing the export user experience: a three-phase status display (preparing, composing, packaging), cycling status messages, and a progress bar from 0% (start) to 100% (download ready).
  • AvatarSwitcher / SkeletonCanvas (Feature: animate-avatar): AvatarSwitcher allows selecting between four VRM models; SkeletonCanvas provides a 2D Canvas fallback rendering raw pose landmarks for inspection. Satisfies FR009, FR011.
  • usePlayback (Feature: animate-avatar): Manages animation sequence state: idle, playing, paused, complete. Provides play, pause, replay, previous/next token, and speed cycling (0.5×–2×). Satisfies FR008.
  • useHistory (Shared): localStorage-based translation history with FIFO eviction at 100 entries. Supports filtering by type, date range, and search query; tracks export flags. Satisfies FR014.
  • KalidokitSolver / vrmRigger (Shared utilities): Receive normalised landmarks and return VRM-compatible bone rotation quaternions and facial blendshapes. Kalidokit has not received active maintenance since 2022, but it remains the only open-source library that bridges MediaPipe landmark output to VRM bone rotations. No maintained alternative exists for this specific task; the library is stable for the landmark solving requirements of this project.

FastAPI Backend Components. The backend container is decomposed into the following components:

  • TranslateRouter (API Router): Handles POST /api/translate, POST /api/translate/fast, and POST /api/translate/stream requests. Validates input text (1–500 characters), invokes the GlossEngine, and returns gloss tokens with method and confidence metadata. The streaming endpoint returns an SSE channel with an immediate rule_based event and an optional llm_quality improvement event.
  • AudioRouter (API Router): Handles POST /api/translate/audio. Accepts multipart audio uploads, forwards the file to the Groq Whisper API (whisper-large-v3-turbo), and feeds the transcription into the GlossEngine. Supports BCP-47 language hints. Satisfies FR002.
  • VocabularyRouter (API Router): Handles GET /api/vocabulary and GET /api/vocabulary/s Loads the gloss index from glosses.tsv and exposes prefix-based search for client-side autocomplete and lexicon checking.
  • MediaRouter (API Router): Handles GET /api/pose/{gloss} and GET /api/video/{gloss}, serving binary .pose and .mp4 assets from the bucket directory with HTTP cache headers (Cache-Control: max-age=86400).
  • ExportRouter (API Router): Handles POST /api/export/video. Accepts either a WebM blob or a JSON array of base64 JPEG frames, invokes FFmpeg via imageio-ffmpeg for H.264 MP4 encoding, and returns the binary MP4 response. Satisfies FR012.
  • GlossEngine (Core Service): The rule-based NLP pipeline using spaCy for tokenisation, lemmatisation, and Part-of-Speech tagging, followed by ASL grammar transformations: temporal topicalisation, subject-object-verb reordering, article and copula removal, and negation repositioning. Pronoun IX-marker8 substitution maps I/you/he to IX-1/IX-2/IX-3. When confidence falls below 0.8, the engine fires an async LLM quality-check using the Groq API for improved output. Satisfies FR003, FR004.
  • FingerspellEngine (Core Service): Called when a gloss token has no matching pose asset in the vocabulary. Decomposes the word into individual ASL alphabet letters and produces a sequence of letter gloss tokens (e.g., “Netflix” → N-E-T-F-L-I-X). Satisfies FR006.
  • Authentication and Persistence Layer: The backend includes user registration, JWT-based authentication (bcrypt-hashed passwords, httpOnly cookie tokens), and SQLAlchemy-backed database persistence. These components satisfy FR013–FR015.

3.2 System Design

The system design outlines the detailed blueprint for DuoSign. It translates the high-level architecture into specific design decisions that guide implementation. This section covers the core design principles, the pose playback strategy, the data model, interaction diagrams, user interface design considerations, and security design.

3.2.1 Design Principles

Seven design principles shaped the decisions across architecture, data model, and user interface:

  • Modularity: The system is decomposed into independent, API-connected services for text-to-gloss conversion, pose extraction, avatar animation, and UI rendering. Each service can be developed, tested, deployed, and replaced independently. A researcher can swap the NLP module for a neural machine translation model by conforming to the same API contract, without modifying any other part of the pipeline. This directly satisfies NFR007 (scalability/extensibility).
  • Performance: The system is optimised to ensure that end-to-end translation and initial avatar rendering completes under 2,000 milliseconds for a standard sentence. The .pose file playback strategy (Section 3.2.2) reduces client-side processing by bypass-ing live MediaPipe inference for pre-extracted glosses, enabling consistent 60 FPS playback even on lower-powered devices. This satisfies NFR002.
  • Scalability: The architecture separates stateless NLP processing from stateful user data, allowing each layer to scale independently. The backend handles only lightweight text processing and audio forwarding while all compute-intensive rendering operations run client-side, eliminating server-side video handling entirely. This satisfies NFR007.
  • Accessibility: The user interface provides multiple input modalities (text and voice), includes text transcripts of gloss sequences for users who cannot view animations, supports keyboard navigation, maintains minimum 44×44 pixel touch targets, and meets WCAG AA colour contrast requirements. This satisfies NFR003.
  • Extensibility: The file-based lexicon allows new signs to be added by dropping .pose files into the correct directory with the appropriate gloss identifier, without requiring code changes, redeployment, or retraining. The modular design ensures vocabulary can grow independently of the core pipeline.
  • Data Privacy: Data privacy is enforced at the architecture level; the concrete controls are defined in Section 3.2.6. This satisfies NFR006.
  • Reproducibility: As an open-source baseline system, all architectural decisions prioritise transparency and replicability. The fully open-source codebase, documented API contracts, and standardised data formats allow other researchers to replicate results and extend the system.
3.2.2 Video-Driven Avatar Playback and Pose-Based Skeleton Fallback

The core animation design in DuoSign separates live avatar rendering from precomputed skeletal reference data. Sign videos from the WLASL dataset [23] are the primary animation source: the browser fetches each video from Supabase Storage CDN, plays it through a hidden <video> element, and sends decoded frames through the MediaPipe Tasks Vision HolisticLandmarker running as WebAssembly. The resulting landmark arrays (33 body joints, 21 left-hand joints, and 21 right-hand joints) are fed into Kalidokit, which solves them into VRM bone rotation quaternions applied in a requestAnimationFrame loop at 60 FPS. This is the useVideoEngine path, grounded directly in recordings of real signers from the WLASL corpus [23].

The limitation of this approach is the Kalidokit solver itself. Automated landmark-to-bone conversion does not always produce a visually correct sign: perspective issues in the source video, partial occlusion of hands, or quaternion discontinuities between frames can cause the avatar to hold an unnatural pose for a token. To address this, DuoSign includes a skeleton overlay path. Offline, each sign video in the WLASL dataset was processed through the same MediaPipe pipeline and the resulting landmark data was serialised into a compact binary .pose file, one per gloss. The SkeletonCanvas component reads these files and renders the raw 2D skeleton alongside the VRM avatar when the user toggles skeleton view. This gives a ground-truth reference of what the sign should look like at the landmark level, independent of the avatar’s quaternion interpretation.

In practice: the VRM avatar plays the sign in 3D; the skeleton canvas shows what MediaPipe actually extracted from the source video. Where they match, the sign is correct. Where they diverge, the skeleton is the reliable one. See Figure 3.5.

Implementation constraint: direct .pose driving of the avatar. During implementation, I tested whether the avatar could be driven directly from precomputed .pose files instead of streaming source video frames through MediaPipe and Kalidokit. In practice, this path was not stable. The pose structures produced by the Python pose-format tooling did not align cleanly with the frame structure expected by Kalidokit’s MediaPipe-oriented reader in the browser.

To verify this, I reverse-engineered the runtime data path: landmark frames passed through the Kalidokit media flow were extracted to JSON and then fed back into the avatar rigging path. The result was consistently poor, including jittery movement, unnaturally fast playback, and frame-timing errors that broke the natural signing rhythm. By contrast, the video-stream path preserves the frame cadence Kalidokit was designed for, because it matches the library’s original real-time camera input assumptions. For this reason, DuoSign keeps video-driven avatar animation as the primary path and uses .pose files for skeleton reference and fallback rendering.

Coordinate-system normalisation as an architectural decision. A cross-cutting design constraint in this pipeline is coordinate-system compatibility between MediaPipe and Three.js/VRM. MediaPipe emits landmarks in normalised screen space (origin top-left) where the Y-axis increases downward, while Three.js/VRM rigs assume world space where Y increases upward. Without correction, vertical motion is inverted during retargeting. DuoSign therefore applies a boundary transformation before Kalidokit/VRM rigging:

𝑦′ = 1.0 − 𝑦 (3.1)

where 𝑦 is the MediaPipe Y-coordinate and 𝑦′ is the corrected Y-coordinate in the avatar coordinate frame. This normalisation is enforced at the landmark-to-rig interface for both runtime video landmarking and precomputed .pose playback, so downstream animation logic operates in a single consistent coordinate space.

3.2.3 Data Model

Current Prototype State (localStorage). In the current DuoSign prototype, persistent state is held in browser-local stores rather than a server-side database. Translation history is serialized to localStorage under a dedicated key by the useHistory hook. Each history entry stores the original input text, gloss token sequence (JSON array), input type ("typed" or "voice"), display-oriented date fields, and an export flag. A FIFO10 policy caps history at 100 entries. User preferences, including avatar model selection, color accent, animation speed, accessibility toggles, and voice settings, are serialized separately by SettingsProvider through the useSettings hook and rehydrated on page load.

Guest usage tracking uses a session-based browser identifier: the useGuestBanner hook maintains a translation count in localStorage and displays a soft registration prompt when the configured threshold is reached. No hashed identifier or server record is created in the prototype.

Production Database Schema. The production schema has four tables. users stores registered accounts with UUID11 primary keys and bcrypt-hashed passwords (FR013). sessions manages JWT refresh tokens with cascading delete on account removal. guest_usage records a one-way hashed browser identifier and translation count, never raw IP addresses or personally identifying information (NFR006, NFR017). translations stores translation history for logged-in users: input text, input method, gloss output as a JSONB12 array, and a creation timestamp (FR014–FR015). The schema is designed and migrations are written; deployment requires connecting the Supabase PostgreSQL instance.

Asset Storage Structure. In the current prototype, sign language media assets are stored in a bucket/ directory mounted beside the application. The structure separates raw videos (one .mp4 clip per gloss class, selected by quality score from the WLASL dataset [23]) from precomputed .pose files. A gloss_video_mapping.json index maps each gloss name to its selected video and pose asset. In production deployment, this directory is replaced by a Supabase Storage bucket; the FastAPI backend reads the asset base URL from an environment variable, so no code changes are required to switch between local and cloud storage. The /api/pose/{gloss} and /api/video/{gloss} endpoints serve binary asset responses with HTTP cache headers (Cache-Control: max-age=86400), allowing browsers to avoid refetching commonly used signs. A /avatars/ directory within the Next.js public/ folder hosts the four VRM avatar models.

3.2.4 Interaction Diagrams

Activity diagrams document the dynamic behaviour of the four most important system flows.

3.2.4.1 Full Translation Pipeline Activity

The primary activity diagram outlines the complete translation pipeline from text input to avatar animation. See Figure 3.7. The process begins when a user submits English text, either typed or transcribed from voice input. The text is sent to the FastAPI backend via POST /api/translate/stream using Server-Sent Events. The backend immediately fires the spaCy rule-based pipeline and emits a rule_based event with the initial gloss tokens. If the confidence score is below 0.8 or the sentence contains idiomatic patterns, an asynchronous LLM quality check is fired; if the LLM responds within a configurable timeout, an llm_quality event is emitted with the improved result. A done event signals completion.

Upon receiving the gloss token array, the frontend iterates through each token sequentially. For each token, the useVideoEngine hook fetches the source sign video from Supabase Storage CDN, plays it through a hidden <video> element, and pipes decoded frames through MediaPipe Tasks Vision to drive the VRM in real time. If no source video is found for the token, useVideoEngine delegates to usePosePlayer as the fallback: the hook checks an in-memory Map cache for pre-parsed frame data; on a cache miss it fetches the .pose binary file, parses it, caches it, and drives the VRM from the precomputed landmark sequences. If neither asset exists for a word, the FingerspellEngine decomposes it into individual letter tokens. After all tokens have played, the system checks the guest usage counter in localStorage and, if exceeded, displays a soft registration prompt. The translation entry is automatically appended to the localStorage history store.

3.2.4.2 Voice Input Flow

The voice input flow branches from the main translation pipeline and covers both microphone paths. See Figure 3.8. The user clicks the microphone icon in the translation interface. The frontend first attempts to use the Web Speech API. If the browser supports it and microphone permission is granted, native speech recognition starts; the interface enters a listening state with visual feedback, the user speaks, and the browser returns a local transcription. The text is inserted into the input field for review before submission. From there, the flow is identical to typed input.

If the Web Speech API is unavailable or if the user chooses the alternative voice path, the frontend instead initiates a MediaRecorder session. The user speaks and the browser captures the audio as a .webm blob. On stop, the frontend uploads the blob to POST /api/translate/audio with an optional BCP-47 language hint. The backend forwards the audio to the Groq Whisper API, retrieves the transcription, passes it through the GlossEngine, and returns the gloss tokens directly. The transcribed text is displayed to the user alongside the avatar animation.

3.2.4.3 Guest-to-Registered User Conversion Flow

Guest users are tracked by a session-based browser identifier stored in localStorage. When a guest reaches the configured translation threshold, a soft registration prompt appears after the current translation completes. Figure 3.9 shows this conversion flow. Registration is optional and appears only after the user has received value. The prompt offers two choices: create a free account or continue as a guest with reduced access. If dismissed, the user continues in limited mode. If accepted, the user completes a short form (email and password). On success, a JWT is issued in an httpOnly cookie, and the user returns to the translation screen without losing current input. History from that point is stored server-side; previous guest history is not migrated.

3.2.4.4 Video Export Flow

The video export flow allows users to download an MP4 recording of the avatar signing a translated gloss sequence. See Figure 3.10. The user clicks the Export button in the avatar panel or on a history entry. The frontend opens the ExportVideoModal, which renders a hidden AvatarCanvas and immediately begins recording via useCanvasRecorder.

Two recording paths are used based on browser capability. In Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, canvas.captureStream(30) produces a MediaStream fed to a MediaRecorder at 8 Mbps, producing a .webm blob. In Safari, where captureStream is unsupported, JPEG frames are sampled at 15 fps via canvas.toDataURL and accumulated as a base64 array. Once the animation sequence completes and the recording stops, the blob or frame array is uploaded to POST /api/export/video. The FastAPI backend transcodes the input to H.264 MP4 at 1280×720, CRF 18, with +faststart, using the bundled imageio-ffmpeg binary. The resulting MP4 is returned to the client, which creates a blob URL and triggers download as duosign-export.mp4. The history entry for this translation is marked as exported. This flow satisfies FR012.

3.2.5 User Interface Design

The interface was designed for the five user groups identified in Chapter 2: deaf and hard-of-hearing users, hearing users communicating with deaf colleagues, ASL learners, content creators, and researchers. These groups use the same translation screen for different goals. Wireframes were developed in Figma, and representative screens are included in Appendix B.

Layout Principles. The interface follows a two-panel structure: input on the left (or top on mobile viewports) and avatar output on the right (or bottom). This mirrors the interaction pattern of successful translation tools such as Google Translate and ensures spatial separation between where the user acts and where the system responds. The layout is responsive and adapts to desktop (≥1024 px: two-column grid), tablet, and mobile (<1024 px: stacked column with sticky input panel) viewport sizes.

Typography. The design system employs three typefaces, each serving a distinct purpose: Instrument Serif for the DuoSign logo and brand identity, Work Sans Bold for headings and all-caps labels, and Inter Regular for body text and UI elements. This combination provides clear visual hierarchy while maintaining readability across screen sizes.

Key Components. The translation page comprises three primary panels. The Input Panel contains the text input area (maximum 500 characters), a state-aware microphone button, a submit button, and a character count indicator. The Avatar Panel contains the Three.js canvas rendering the VRM avatar, loading state indicators, playback controls (play, pause, previous/next token, replay, speed cycle), display mode selector (avatar, skeleton, hidden), view mode selector (close-up, full body, 3D world), avatar model switcher, export button, and a fullscreen toggle. The Gloss Panel displays token chips horizontally, with the active token highlighted during playback and a distinct visual treatment for fingerspelled words. Every interactive element is designed with four explicit states: default, hover, active/pressed, and disabled. The avatar panel requires additional loading, playing, paused, and error states.

Accessibility Considerations. The avatar panel includes a text transcript of the gloss sequence for users who cannot view the animation. All interactive elements support keyboard navigation with a minimum 44×44 pixel touch target. Colour contrast meets WCAG AA as a minimum. The voice input button uses shape change rather than colour alone to indicate state, ensuring usability for users with colour vision deficiency.

3.2.6 Security Design

Security is a cross-cutting concern that informs decisions across all layers of the architecture. The security design for DuoSign addresses API protection, data privacy, and guest tracking.

Authentication. JWT access tokens are issued on login and stored in httpOnly cookies rather than localStorage, preventing browser scripts from reading them. Access tokens expire after 24 hours with refresh token rotation on renewal. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (minimum 12 rounds) before storage.

API Security. The FastAPI backend enables CORS13 only for explicitly configured development and deployment origins. All text inputs are validated through Pydantic request models before entering the NLP pipeline. Translation endpoints are rate-limited to 60 requests per minute per IP address to reduce abuse.

Data Privacy. Video frames used for avatar landmarking are processed client-side via WebAssembly; no raw video reaches the backend. Voice input follows two paths. With Web Speech API, transcription stays in the browser and audio does not leave the device. With Groq Whisper, spoken audio is sent to FastAPI, forwarded for transcription, and then discarded; only text proceeds. Translation history is stored in localStorage; no personal interaction data is retained on the server beyond each request.

Guest Tracking. Guest usage identifiers are one-way hashed before server-side storage. The server stores only a count and timestamp, never a raw IP address or personally identifying information.

3.3 Deployment Architecture

This section describes how DuoSign is deployed beyond a local development machine, mapping each component in the container diagram to a hosting provider. The choices are deliberately aligned with the project’s constraints: everything runs within free or low-cost tiers, no dedicated infrastructure management is required, and the entire system can be reproduced by anyone following this documentation.

3.3.1 Hosting Stack

Table 3.1 summarises the production hosting plan for each container.

Table 3.1. DuoSign production hosting stack.
ContainerProviderPlanMonthly Cost
Next.js FrontendVercelHobby (free)$0
FastAPI BackendRenderFree / Starter$0–$7
Media Asset StoreSupabase StorageFree (100 GB)$0
PostgreSQL DatabaseSupabaseFree (500 MB DB)$0
LLM + WhisperGroq APIPay-as-you-go<$1

Next.js Frontend — Vercel. Vercel is the natural deployment target for Next.js applications: it is built by the same team, requires zero configuration for App Router projects, and provides a global CDN with automatic HTTPS on its free Hobby plan. Each git push to the main branch triggers an automatic deployment. Static assets and JavaScript bundles are served from Vercel’s edge network; only API calls leave the browser to reach the FastAPI backend.

FastAPI Backend — Render. The FastAPI service is deployed on Render, a platform-as-a-service provider for Python web services. A render.yaml file at the repository root defines the build command (pip install -r requirements.txt) and start command (uvicorn main:app –host 0.0.0.0 –port $PORT). The Python environment and dependencies, including spaCy and the bundled FFmpeg binary from imageio-ffmpeg, are installed at build time, so no system-level packages are required on the host.

Media Asset Store — Supabase Storage. Sign language reference videos, precomputed .pose files, and VRM avatar models are stored in Supabase Storage. Supabase provides 100 GB on the free plan, an S3-compatible API, built-in CDN delivery, and public asset URLs. Because Supabase also hosts PostgreSQL, storage and database remain under one platform and one credential scope. At this project scale, roughly 2,500 sign videos at about 1.5 MB each plus matching .pose files remain well within the free tier. The FastAPI backend reads asset paths from environment variables pointing to Supabase public URLs.

Capacity Estimate. At 100 simultaneous users making one translation request per minute, the FastAPI backend receives about 100 requests per minute. Each request is lightweight, with text input and JSON gloss output, so one Render Starter instance (512 MB RAM, shared CPU) is sufficient. Media assets are fetched directly from Supabase CDN by the browser, so these requests do not load the FastAPI backend. Supabase free-tier egress is 5 GB per month; estimated usage at this traffic level is about 1.5 GB per month, which stays within the free allowance.

3.3.2 Scalability Considerations

The current deployment is sized for a small user base, up to about 100 concurrent users, which fits this academic implementation. Scaling does not require structural redesign; the path is horizontal. The FastAPI backend is stateless and keeps no in-memory session state between requests, so additional Render instances can be placed behind a load balancer without code changes. The frontend is already distributed through Vercel’s CDN. Media storage scales through Supabase plan upgrades or migration to Cloudflare R214.

Microservices, Kubernetes, and container orchestration are intentionally outside the scope of this project. One FastAPI process handles translation, audio, vocabulary, media, and export endpoints together. This keeps operations simple for a research prototype and avoids infrastructure overhead that is unnecessary at the current scale. If demand increases, the modular design still allows service-level separation later.

3.4 Summary

This chapter has presented DuoSign’s architecture and design using three C4 levels. It detailed the modular pipeline, the split between server-side NLP and client-side pose extraction/rendering, and the rationale behind these choices. It also documented the FSD frontend, FastAPI backend, pose playback strategy with .pose fallback, storage and deployment setup, and the main interaction flows (translation, voice, registration, and export). The chapter closes with interface and security design decisions tied to Chapter 2 requirements.

Throughout the chapter, design decisions were mapped to Chapter 2 requirements: the FSD frontend supports FR001 (translation interface), FR014 (history), and FR009 (display modes); the FastAPI NLP service supports FR003 (text-to-gloss) and FR002 (voice transcription); the pose playback strategy supports FR005 (avatar animation) and FR008 (playback controls); the dual-path voice design supports FR002 while addressing privacy trade-offs; the export flow supports FR012; and authentication plus persistence design support FR013–FR015. Together, these decisions form the implementation blueprint used in Chapter 4.

  1. WebAssembly = A low-level binary instruction format that enables near-native performance in web ↩︎
  2. SSE = Server-Sent Events, a unidirectional HTTP streaming mechanism for incremental server updates. ↩︎
  3. C4 = Context, Containers, Components, and Code; a hierarchical model for communicating software architecture. ↩︎
  4. H.264 = Advanced Video Coding (AVC), a widely used video compression standard. ↩︎
  5. IX = Index marker in sign-language gloss notation, used to represent pointing pronouns and referential indexing in signing space. ↩︎
  6. FIFO = First In, First Out. ↩︎
  7. UUID = Universally Unique Identifier. ↩︎
  8. JSONB = Binary JSON storage format in PostgreSQL that supports indexing and efficient querying. ↩︎
  9. CORS = Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, a browser security mechanism controlling cross-origin HTTP requests. ↩︎
  10. R2 = Cloudflare’s object storage service with S3-compatible APIs. ↩︎

Chapter 4 Implementation

This chapter explains how DuoSign was built in practice. Rather than restating the full architecture from Chapter 3, it focuses on implementation-level decisions: the tools actually used, how the main subsystems were assembled, and the practical trade-offs made during development.

4.1 Software, Tools, and Technologies

DuoSign uses the stack described in Chapter 3 (Section 3.1). This chapter therefore records only implementation-specific observations that affected development rather than re-listing each framework in full.

The most important frontend observation was performance: the Three.js scene typically required about 400–600 ms to initialise, which shaped loading behaviour and justified progressive interface feedback while the avatar renderer became interactive. A second practical finding was that Kalidokit remained useful as a bridge between MediaPipe landmarks and VRM bone rotations, but its maintenance status and solver artefacts meant that some signs still required manual tuning and careful debugging during playback.

4.2 Software Development Approach

DuoSign was built through a solo adaptation of Agile development. Work was organised into short implementation cycles, with each cycle producing a usable increment that could be tested before the next subsystem was added. This mattered because several decisions — especially around pose driving, avatar playback, export, and deployment —only became clear after working prototypes were exercised end to end.

In practice, development prioritised a minimal usable pipeline first and then improved each subsystem in cycles. This kept the work responsive to technical uncertainty while preserving a modular structure: frontend and backend responsibilities stayed clearly separated, features were added in layers, and interfaces were kept stable enough to support debugging, testing, and later extension.

4.3 Implementation Details

DuoSign is built and integrated using multiple interacting components. This section details the technical execution of each component, covering project structure, the text-to-gloss translation engine, WLASL video acquisition and pose extraction, the avatar animation system, video export, user interfaces, and security considerations.

4.3.1 Project File Structure

The DuoSign system is organised into a modular file structure that separates offline data processing scripts from the runtime application code.

The frontend follows the Feature-Sliced Design described in Chapter 3 (Section 3.1.1.1), so the implementation focus here is how that structure supported the finished repository layout rather than re-explaining the pattern.

The complete project structure is as follows:

This organisation enforces a strict dependency rule: layers may only import from layers below them in the hierarchy (app → widgets → features → entities → shared), preventing circular dependencies and ensuring that domain logic remains decoupled from presentation.

4.3.2 Client State and Asset Storage

The storage split introduced earlier in this chapter is reflected directly in the runtime implementation. Translation history and user preferences remain in browser localStorage, while reusable sign videos and .pose assets are loaded from the shared media bucket.

At runtime, the main implementation concern is not persistence itself but retrieval efficiency: media routes emit cache headers, and parsed landmark data is reused in memory to reduce repeated processing during playback.

4.3.3 Text-to-Gloss Translation Engine

The text-to-gloss translation engine forms the core NLP component of DuoSign, converting standard English text into ASL gloss notation. The engine is implemented in text_to_gloss.py as a FastAPI service with three processing stages: text normalisation, grammatical transformation, and lexicon validation.

4.3.3.1 Text Normalisation

The normalisation stage cleans raw input text to produce a consistent token stream. Operations include lowercasing, punctuation removal, and contraction expansion (e.g., “don’t” → “do not”, “won’t” → “will not”). The expanded forms ensure that subsequent POS tagging and dependency parsing operate on complete grammatical structures rather than contracted forms that may be ambiguously tagged.

4.3.3.2 Grammatical Transformation

The grammatical transformation stage converts English word order and structure into ASL-appropriate gloss sequences using spaCy’s dependency parser and POS tagger. The rule-based system applies three principal transformations:

  • Reordering: English’s Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order is transformed to ASL’s Time-Topic-Comment structure. Temporal markers are fronted to the beginning of the gloss sequence (e.g., “I went to the store yesterday” → YESTERDAY STORE I GO).
  • Dropping: Articles (a, an, the) and copulas (is, am, are) are removed where appropriate, as these do not have direct equivalents in ASL grammar.
  • Pronoun and Synonym Mapping: Personal pronouns are converted to IX (Index) markers (I → IX-1, you → IX-2, he/she → IX-3, we → IX-1+, they → IX-3+) for spatial reference in ASL [32]. Words not present in the lexicon are mapped to known synonyms (e.g., “wealthy” → RICH, “automobile” → CAR). A confidence score is computed as the proportion of output tokens that have known

gloss assets. When this falls below 0.8 or idiomatic patterns are detected, an asynchronous LLM quality check fires against the Groq API and, if it responds within the configured timeout, an improved result is emitted as a second SSE event.

4.3.3.3 Lexicon Validation and Fallback

Each produced gloss token is validated against the loaded vocabulary, sourced from glosses.tsv and the bucket’s gloss mapping. The validation follows a three-tier fallback strategy:

  1. Direct match: The gloss class name exists in the vocabulary and has an associated pose asset.
  2. Synonym fallback: If the primary gloss is missing, the system checks known synonyms before escalating.
  3. Fingerspelling fallback: If no gloss class match or synonym is found, the system decomposes the word into individual letters and produces a sequence of fingerspelling tokens using the ASL manual alphabet (e.g., “Netflix” → N-E-T-F-L-I-X).
4.3.3.4 Algorithm: Text-to-Gloss Conversion Pipeline

Algorithm 1 formalises the TextToGloss.convert() method that drives every translation request. Its high-level structure is adapted in part from the open-source SignMT workflow reported by Moryossef et al. [26], particularly in the separation of conversion stages and fallback logic, although the concrete rules and runtime paths used here are specific to DuoSign. The two-path design — rule-based first, LLM only when needed — gives the system its responsiveness: the rule-based path completes in under 50 ms, so most requests return immediately. The background quality check fires concurrently and, if it returns within the 3-second timeout, upgrades the result silently over the SSE channel.

Algorithm 2 details the rule-based sub-pipeline. The key design decision is that tokens are kept in their original parse order throughout filtering and glossification; reordering is applied as a series of targeted structural moves rather than by decomposing the sentence into category buckets. This preserves modifier–noun relationships automatically — an adjective already beside its noun requires no special rule to stay there after SOV reordering.

4.3.4 WLASL Pose Extraction Pipeline

With the downloaded video corpus established, the offline processing workflow transformed each short clip into a structured landmark tensor suitable for avatar animation at runtime. This preprocessing stage is conceptually separate from the shipped runtime: the frontend consumes prepared .pose assets and only invokes MediaPipe Tasks Vision when animating directly from source videos in the browser.

4.3.4.1 Pipeline Architecture

The extraction pipeline follows a multi-stage architecture with parallelised execution. Eight worker processes operated concurrently, each maintaining its own MediaPipe Holistic instance to avoid shared state. Video frames were decoded sequentially, landmarked, scored for quality, and serialised into reusable pose assets. The important interface between offline extraction and online playback is that offline processing produces fixed-shape landmark data; online playback either parses those .pose files into frame arrays, or derives equivalent landmark sets on the fly via the browser HolisticLandmarker. In both cases, Kalidokit receives a consistent landmark structure for rig solving.

For each video, the pipeline proceeded through the following stages:

  1. Video decoding: OpenCV’s VideoCapture interface opened the video file, extracted frame rate and frame count metadata, and emitted frames one at a time as RGB numpy arrays. BGR-to-RGB colour space conversion was applied at read time, as MediaPipe’s inference graph expects RGB input.
  2. Landmark detection: MediaPipe Holistic processed each frame, returning pose, face, and hand landmarks. Missing regions were represented explicitly so that frame shapes remained consistent across videos with partial detection.
  3. Landmark reduction: The 33-point BlazePose skeleton was reduced to 13 upper-body landmarks: nose (index 0), left and right shoulders (11, 12), elbows (13, 14), wrists (15, 16), and the hand-to-wrist connection points—pinky, index, and thumb tips (17–22). Lower-body landmarks (hips, knees, ankles, feet) were discarded, as sign language articulation is exclusively performed by the upper body. This reduction produced a final layout of 523 landmarks per frame: 13 pose + 468 face + 21 left hand + 21 right hand.
  4. Quality scoring: A composite quality metric 𝑄 was computed for each video:

𝑄 = 0.30 · 𝑟pose + 0.25 · 𝑟face + 0.20 · 𝑟¯hands + 0.15 · 𝑐¯ + 0.10 · 𝑐complete (4.1)

where 𝑟pose is the pose detection rate, 𝑟face is the face detection rate, 𝑟¯hands is the mean bilateral hand detection rate, 𝑐¯ is the mean per-landmark confidence, and 𝑐complete is the proportion of frames where all four regions were simultaneously detected. Videos failing to achieve a minimum pose detection rate of 70% were excluded from candidacy.

  1. Serialisation: The assembled landmark tensor of shape (𝑇 × 523 × 4)—encoding (𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧, visibility) per landmark per frame—was written to disk as a compressed NumPy archive with the .pose extension. Atomic writes were used: data was first written to a .tmp temporary file, then renamed, guaranteeing that a crash during serialisation could not produce a corrupted output file.
4.3.4.2 Performance Results

The pipeline was run to completion on an Apple MacBook M4 Pro without requiring cloud compute. The following metrics were recorded:

Table 4.1. WLASL Pose Extraction Pipeline Performance
MetricValue
Total videos processed 11,980
Processing time 4,548 seconds (≈76 minutes)
Success rate100%
Average throughput 2.6 videos/second
Worker processes 8 (parallel)
Memory per worker <500 MB

The Apple Neural Engine’s deep learning acceleration contributed measurably to the 2.6 videos/second throughput.

4.3.4.3 Quality-Based Pose Selection

Following extraction, the selection script consumed the quality scores per video and selected the single highest-scoring representative for each gloss class. The important point is that selection does not introduce a second weighting scheme: it reuses the same composite metric defined in Equation 4.1. All candidate videos for a given gloss were therefore scored during extraction, then sorted by the same score 𝑄 before the winner was checked against the minimum acceptance threshold. The top-ranked candidate was designated the primary animation asset, while lower-ranked alternatives that remained reasonably close in quality were retained as fallbacks. This produced a flat dictionary keyed by gloss name, containing the selected video identifier, detection rates, confidence average, and composite rank score. This mapping file serves as the runtime lexicon index consulted by the frontend before initiating any animation request.

Algorithm 3 formalises this ranking stage explicitly as a reuse of the extraction-time quality metric rather than a separate selection-specific formula. Pose and face reliability remain explicit, but hand visibility is aggregated bilaterally as 𝑟¯hands, while 𝑐¯ and 𝑐complete preserve information about landmark confidence and full-frame completeness during ranking.

4.3.5 Pose Serialisation and Runtime Loading

The runtime code consumes binary .pose files directly. The frontend’s usePosePlayer hook fetches a .pose asset from /api/pose/{gloss}, parses the binary structure in JavaScript into per-frame landmark arrays, and caches the result in an in-memory Map for reuse within the page session. This design removes an extra transformation step from the delivery pipeline: a pose file is fetched once, parsed, and then replayed at a target frame rate while Kalidokit solves upper-body pose, both hands, and facial motion for each frame. If a gloss has no corresponding pose asset, the player degrades gracefully by briefly holding the current pose rather than breaking the sequence.

Alongside this pose-player path, the useVideoEngine hook provides a video-driven landmarking alternative. That hook fetches an .mp4 gloss video, processes each frame through MediaPipe Tasks Vision HolisticLandmarker in the browser, and applies the resulting landmarks to the same VRM rigging pipeline. The system therefore supports both precomputed-pose playback and video-driven landmarking through a shared animation interface.

For architectural consistency, the coordinate-system design decision is documented in Chapter 3 (Section 3.2.2) and implemented unchanged in this runtime path.

4.3.6 Avatar Rendering and Animation

This layer renders signing motion in real time and keeps playback stable across desktop and mobile browsers. For each frame, landmark inputs are converted into avatar motion and applied continuously in the render loop.

Users can switch between close-up, full-body, and 3D world camera views depending on readability needs. A skeleton display mode provides a simplified landmark view, and a lightweight stats overlay supports runtime debugging during development.

4.3.6.1 Kalidokit Limitations in Practice

Kalidokit was a useful starting point for getting the avatar pipeline working, and it made it possible to turn pose landmarks into visible signing motion in the browser. In practice, though, it was not equally smooth or reliable for every sign. Simpler signs worked better, while more complex handshapes, palm orientation, contact points, and rest positions were less consistent. For this reason, DuoSign uses the VRM stack that proved most stable with Kalidokit in the final implementation, but the limits of that setup are part of why smoother signing remains future work. A fuller discussion of these limitations appears in Chapter 6, while the appendix provides both the parameter-level matrix (Appendix G) and a short implementation findings matrix (Appendix H).

4.3.7 Video Export Pipeline

DuoSign implements client-to-server avatar recording that converts a live signing animation into a downloadable MP4 file. The implementation spans three interacting components: the ExportVideoModal React component, the useCanvasRecorder hook, and the POST /api/export/video FastAPI endpoint.

4.3.7.1 Client-Side Canvas Capture

When the user clicks Export, the export modal renders a hidden 16:9 avatar canvas and passes that canvas to the recorder hook. The browser then chooses the most suitable capture method automatically: browsers with standard canvas-stream support use captureStream() and MediaRecorder to record the animation directly, while Safari and iOS fall back to frame-by-frame JPEG capture for later server conversion. In both cases, the modal coordinates recording and playback so that capture starts slightly before animation begins and ends with a short delay after playback, preserving the full signed sequence in the exported result.

4.3.7.2 Server-Side FFmpeg Conversion

The captured media is uploaded to the export endpoint as multipart form data, where the backend converts it to a downloadable MP4 file. Standard browsers usually send a recorded WebM stream, while Safari-style fallback capture sends a sequence of JPEG frames; both inputs are normalised through the same FFmpeg-based packaging step with web-compatible H.264 settings. Because the service uses a bundled FFmpeg binary, deployment does not depend on a separate host-level FFmpeg installation.

4.3.7.3 User Experience

The modal displays three phases of cycling status messages: preparing (while the VRM loads), composing (during animation playback), and packaging (during server-side FFmpeg conversion). A continuous progress bar runs from 0% (start of recording) to 55% (end of playback) to 100% (download ready), giving users meaningful feedback without polling the server. The close button is disabled during recording and processing to prevent accidental cancellation. This implementation satisfies FR012.

4.3.8 User Interfaces and Functionalities

The user interface provides the primary interaction surface for DuoSign. The design prioritises clarity, accessibility, and immediate feedback. The current implementation delivers four distinct pages within the Next.js web application: landing, translation, history, and settings.

4.3.8.1 Translation Interface

The main translation view adopts a two-panel layout: on desktop (≥1024 px), the InputPanel occupies the left column and the AvatarPanel occupies the right; on mobile, the panels stack vertically with the input panel sticky at the bottom. On submission, the frontend calls POST /api/translate/stream via SSE, receives an immediate rule-based gloss sequence, and may later receive an LLM-refined update over the same channel. Gloss tokens are rendered as GlossChip components with the active token highlighted during playback. Playback controls (play, pause, previous/next token, replay, speed cycle) and display mode controls (avatar, skeleton, hidden; close-up, full body, 3D world) are embedded within the AvatarPanel widget.

4.3.8.2 Avatar Customisation

Users can switch avatar models and visual preferences directly from the interface. The selected model is loaded into the avatar canvas, while colour and appearance settings are applied from the settings panel. A skeleton mode is also available for learners who want a simplified landmark view. Together, these features support FR005, FR009, FR010, and FR011.

4.3.8.3 Translation History

The history view is implemented entirely on the client side via the useHistory hook. It displays previously translated phrases grouped by date (Today, Yesterday, and named dates), with each entry showing input type icon, input text, timestamp, and metadata badges (gloss count, input type, exported status). Entries are expandable to reveal gloss token chips and action buttons: Replay (pushes saved text back to the translate route and auto-plays), Export (opens ExportVideoModal for any history entry), Edit (pre-fills input on translate page), and Delete. Filtering is available by date range (Today, This Week, This Month, All Time), input type (Typed, Voice), and free-text search. An “Exported” segment control limits the view to entries that have been exported as video. This satisfies FR014.

4.3.8.4 Settings Interface

The settings page exposes application preferences through a local-only control surface organised into sidebar-navigated sections. A Save/Discard mechanism tracks dirty state and provides visual confirmation on save.

4.4 Integration of Components

The integration of DuoSign’s components follows the API contracts defined in Chapter 3. In practice, the frontend calls a small set of FastAPI endpoints that handle translation, voice transcription, vocabulary lookup, media retrieval, export, and health checks. The exact routes are documented in the architecture diagrams, so they are not repeated here.

The runtime flow is straightforward: user input is sent from the frontend to the backend, gloss output is returned and rendered as chips, and the playback layer fetches the required pose or video assets for animation. Kalidokit then maps landmark data to VRM bone rotations in the avatar renderer. This split keeps language processing, animation, and asset management loosely coupled, which supports NFR007 (scalability) and NFR008 (maintainability).

Chapter 5 Testing and Results

5.1 Introduction

This chapter reports how DuoSign was tested and evaluated across three areas: component-level software testing, accessibility compliance, and a small human-centred pilot study. Because the user-study dataset remained limited, the findings are presented as formative pilot results rather than as evidence from a full confirmatory study.

The evaluation was guided by three core hypotheses:

  1. H1: DuoSign achieves a perceived sign recognition accuracy of at least 80% as reported by participants.
  2. H2: A majority of participants prefer the animated avatar/the 2D skeleton over a plain text or gloss-token display.
  3. H3: Participants recorded a System Usability Scale (SUS) score above 68 (above-average usability).

A total of 124 automated tests were run across the DuoSign backend and frontend, and all 124 passed.

5.4 User Study Design

5.4.1 Ethical Approval and Participants

The study received IRB approval from Ashesi University prior to participant recruitment and data collection. Following approval, demo access links were shared with prospective participants, who were invited to interact with the system and complete a post-session survey.

In total, 36 participants were registered in the study dataset. However, only 5 post-session surveys were submitted and were usable for analysis. This low response rate meant that the findings from the user study were treated as formative pilot results rather than as evidence for broad generalisation.

5.4.2 Instruments

The evaluation used a small set of complementary instruments to capture both numeric and open-ended responses. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was used to measure perceived usability through a standard questionnaire. Likert-scale items captured views on avatar naturalness, output clarity, and transition smoothness. Open-ended questions gave participants space to comment on usability, visual quality, and possible real-world uses of the system.

Taken together, these instruments made it possible to assess not just whether participants found DuoSign usable, but also how they experienced the visual output and where they thought it might be useful.

The mean SUS score of 73.50 is above the standard benchmark of 68 for above-average usability. The five returned SUS scores were 50.0, 77.5, 90.0, 67.5, and 82.5. The scores vary, but they still point to a generally positive usability result.

5.4.5 Expert Sign Review

To complement the participant survey data, an expert domain evaluation, informed by heuristic evaluation principles [27, 41], was carried out with the accessibility team at Ashesi University. Their feedback was qualitative and centred on how easy the avatar output was to interpret; no participant-level recognition percentage was computed in this pilot study. They responded well to the idea behind the project, the overall system design, and the inclusion of the 2D skeleton as a supporting visual aid. Their main concern, however, was the animated avatar itself. They found its signing harder to follow and often relied on the 2D skeleton to confirm the intended sign. Put simply, the overall concept was well received, but the avatar remained the weakest part of the current output pipeline.

5.5 User Acceptance

User acceptance was assessed using SUS scores, willingness-to-use responses, and short free-text comments from the returned hearing-participant surveys. Of those who responded, 60% said they would probably or definitely use DuoSign in a real setting. This suggests cautious but positive acceptance, though the sample is too small and uneven to support broader claims about the target population.

5.6 User Feedback

The returned free-text survey comments, together with the single stored feedback-widget submission, pointed to a few clear themes:

5.6.1 Positive Feedback
  • Interface quality: Respondents described the interface as clean and easy to navigate. One respondent wrote, “IT’S SUCH A LOVELY UI... it’s clean and smooth”.
  • Learning value: Another theme was the system’s potential for self-paced sign-language learning. One respondent stated, “I really appreciate that I can use it to learn sign language at my own pace”.
  • Token and gloss visibility: Users valued the explicit breakdown of words and letters shown by the interface. One respondent noted, “I like how the breakdown of the words and letters is visible”.
5.6.2 Constructive Feedback
  • Avatar motion quality: The most common criticism concerned the readability and fluidity of the avatar. Representative comments included “The avatar’s movements can be a bit difficult to understand” and “The animated avatar is not as fluid so her signing is not really understandable”.
  • Latency and stability: Multiple comments pointed to response time as an immediate issue. One survey response said, “It works slowly and kept freezing”.
5.6.3 Practical Use Contexts Identified

Hearing respondents identified the following real-world contexts in which DuoSign could be practically useful:

  • sign language learning and self-study;
  • lightweight browser-based communication support;
  • classroom or demonstration settings where gloss breakdown helps explain the translation process.

5.7 Discussion

5.7.1 Hypothesis Evaluation

Overall, the evidence offers mixed support for the study hypotheses.

  • H1: This hypothesis was not confirmed. The pilot study did not produce a quantitative perceived-recognition percentage against the 80% target, and the qualitative feedback indicated that the avatar was harder to interpret than expected.
  • H2: This hypothesis was partially supported. Visual output was clearly valued, but the 2D skeleton appeared to be more reliable than the animated avatar for sign verification.
  • H3: This hypothesis was supported within the pilot sample. The mean SUS score of 73.50 was above the standard benchmark of 68, indicating above-average usability. These results suggest that DuoSign works best, for now, as a usable and technically

functional prototype. The clearest area for improvement is avatar quality, especially if stronger claims are to be made about real-world communication effectiveness.

5.7.2 Limitations

The findings in this chapter should be read as pilot results rather than as definitive evidence of real-world performance.

A fuller discussion of the methodological, technical, and communication-related limitations is given in Chapter 6, including the implications of the small sample size, the prototype status of the system, and the gap between technical correctness and practical signing effectiveness.

5.8 Analysis of Test Results

Overall, the results show that DuoSign is a usable and technically sound prototype. It performed well in component testing, met the audited WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility criteria, and achieved an encouraging SUS score. The main weakness was the avatar, especially in terms of clarity and smoothness. So while DuoSign has a solid technical base, it still needs refinement before stronger claims can be made about real-world communication effectiveness.

Chapter 6 Conclusions and Recommendations

DuoSign met its core objectives. This chapter discusses the main limitations, outlines directions for future work, and gives an overall assessment of the project.

6.1 Limitations and Challenges

Although DuoSign met its core objectives as a research prototype, the results in Chapter 5 also show that the system still has some important limitations. Some of these are technical, while others come from the design and scope of the evaluation itself. Together, they affect both the quality of the signing output and the strength of the claims that can reasonably be made from the pilot study.

  • Direct pose-driving constraints: As discussed in Chapter 3 (Section 3.2.2), direct playback of pose files on the avatar was not viable because of frame-timing incompatibilities with Kalidokit. This meant that the intended animation pipeline could not be used in its simplest form and that the final implementation had to rely on a more constrained workaround, which reduced motion fidelity and limited control over avatar behaviour.
  • ASL-only dataset scope: The WLASL corpus is ASL-specific, so DuoSign currently produces ASL-based output regardless of the signing background of the user. This limits the system’s relevance for users in Ghana and other contexts where the dominant signed language is not ASL, since vocabulary, grammar, and sign usage may differ substantially.
  • Avatar solver artefacts: The Kalidokit solver introduced visible artefacts, including quaternion instabilities, distortions from source-video camera-angle variation, and reduced handshape clarity when the hands were partially occluded. These issues affected the readability of the avatar output and were reflected in both participant feedback and expert review.
  • Vocabulary coverage limits: Although fingerspelling provides a complete fallback strategy for out-of-vocabulary items, extended fingerspelled output is slower and harder to interpret than native lexical signing. The 11,980-clip WLASL corpus provides substantial coverage for a prototype, but it does not capture the full vocabulary needed for natural everyday communication, including many names, specialised terms, and longer expressions.
  • Small pilot-study sample: Although 36 participants were registered in the dataset, only 5 usable post-session surveys were returned. This means that the findings should be treated as formative pilot evidence rather than something that can be generalised too widely. The small sample size limits how much can be claimed about usability, preference, and perceived sign-recognition accuracy.
  • Limited evidence for communication effectiveness: The strongest findings on sign quality came from qualitative evidence, especially expert review and participant free-text comments, rather than from large-scale quantitative comprehension measures. This was useful for identifying the main weaknesses in the system, but it does not yet provide enough depth for stronger claims about consistent sign understanding across different users and contexts. Taken together, these limitations suggest that DuoSign is best seen, for now, as a

working research prototype rather than a finished communication system. The platform is technically coherent and usable, but the signing output, linguistic scope, and evaluation base still need more work before stronger claims about real-world deployment can be made.

6.2 Future Work

The next stage of the project should focus on the research and engineering work that would make the system more complete, more locally relevant, and easier to evaluate properly. The priorities below follow directly from the limitations identified during implementation and in the pilot study.

  • Move to a stronger avatar pipeline: One obvious next step is to test alternative avatar rigs or a purpose-built inverse-kinematics solver in place of Kalidokit. In the current system, Kalidokit’s landmark-to-bone mapping introduced artefacts on more complex handshapes and often required manual quaternion correction. A better rigging stack, or a solver trained on sign-language motion data, would likely improve signing quality more directly.
  • Model non-manual grammar more fully: The animation stack should be extended to handle facial grammar more explicitly, including eyebrow movement, eye gaze, mouth morphemes, and head tilt. This is one of the clearest remaining gaps in intelligibility for fluent signers [10, 28].
  • Localise beyond ASL: The project should also move beyond an ASL-only dataset base by extending toward Ghanaian Sign Language (GhSL). This fits the original motivation of the work, which was always tied to low-resource and locally meaningful deployment contexts [37].
  • Expand and repeat the evaluation: Larger and better balanced studies are still needed, ideally with Deaf and hard-of-hearing participants across different fluency levels. Future evaluations should report sentence-level comprehension, task-completion outcomes, and longer-term usability. Publishing reusable protocols and anonymised evaluation artefacts would also make the work easier to reproduce.
  • Improve robustness and domain coverage: The translation pipeline still needs work on harder cases such as idioms, domain-specific terms, code-switching, and long compounds. It would also help to add confidence-aware fallback strategies so users can tell when the system is confident and when the output is only approximate.

6.3 Requirements Compliance and Objective Attainment

DuoSign set out to do three main things: provide sign-first access in a regular web browser, translate English into ASL gloss, and present that output through an animated avatar that people could actually use.

By that standard, the project was largely successful. The browser-based workflow was implemented, the translation pipeline works, and the system supports the main user features discussed earlier in the thesis, including typed and voice input, playback controls, export, and history. The avatar output was also usable, especially for simpler signs such as HELLO, although, as Chapter 5 showed, motion quality was not equally smooth across all signs.

Where the project remains incomplete is in the areas already discussed under limitations. DuoSign does not yet handle richer non-manual grammar well enough, and it has not yet been localised beyond ASL into languages such as GhSL. So while the main system goals were achieved, some of the larger long-term aims still remain future work rather than finished deliverables.

6.4 Conclusion

DuoSign is a useful step toward accessible, hardware-free English-to-ASL communication technology. By combining a hybrid NLP translation pipeline, a pre-processed WLASL pose corpus, and a browser-native 3D avatar renderer, the system shows that real-time sign-language generation can work as a standard web application without specialist infrastructure or device requirements. The evaluation reported in this thesis is still pilot-level, so the main contribution at this stage is the implemented system itself and the reproducible baseline it provides for future studies.

There are still clear weaknesses, especially around avatar expressiveness, dataset language scope, and direct pose-driving constraints. Even so, DuoSign offers a functional open-source baseline for accessible sign-language technology that could be adapted to other signed languages and deployment contexts. The future work identified in this chapter gives a practical path for improving the system so that it can better serve the communicative needs of Deaf communities in Ghana and beyond.

F Application Interface Screenshots

G Kalidokit Retargeting Capability Matrix

Table 6. ASL parameter coverage under the current Kalidokit-VRM retargeting pipeline.
ASL ParameterPipeline CapabilityNotes
Arm location (high/mid/low)ReasonableMain arm position is generally captured.
Arm movement pathReasonableArc and direction are better in video-engine mode.
Simple handshapes (open/closed)PartialGross handshape reproduced; fine distinctions degrade.
Complex handshapesPoorHinge-dominant finger model cannot represent nuanced forms reliably.
Palm orientationPartialFront-facing configurations are stronger than oblique/occluded ones.
Contact precision (chin/temple/chest)PartialContact location can drift in some clips.
Facial grammar (mouth, brows)PoorNot represented with required ASL grammatical fidelity.
Classifier handshape detailPoorFine-grained finger states are under-specified.
Inter-sign natural rest posturePartialNeutral states may appear spread due to Tpose defaults.

H Kalidokit and VRM implementation findings

Table 7. Practical findings from the Kalidokit and VRM implementation used in DuoSign.
ComponentWhat looked promis-ingWhat worked in practiceMain issue / final decision
Kalidokit hand and pose solvingDirect landmark-to-avatar retargeting in the browser without building a custom solver from scratch.Good enough for basic motion and simpler signs, especially when source video quality was strong.Complex handshapes, palm orientation, and contact-heavy signs were less reliable, so the system keeps this as a workable baseline rather than a final solution.
VRM avatar pipelineA ready-made humanoid rig that could be animated inside the browser with standard web graphics tools.The VRM setup allowed real-time signing playback, camera switching, and export from the same rendering pipeline.The final implementation kept the VRM stack that behaved most consistently with Kalidokit, since not every VRM setup produced stable results.
Video-driven landmark pathUsing real source video promised more natural timing and fewer retargeting artefacts than static pose playback alone.This became the main animation path because it preserved the frame cadence Kalidokit han-dled best.It still depends on source-video quality and does not fully solve facial grammar or fine contact precision.
Pose-file fallback pathPrecomputed pose assets promised faster playback and less repeated inference at runtime.Useful as a fallback and for skeleton inspection when direct video playback was unavailable or inconsistent.Motion looked flatter and less natural than the live video path, so it remained a secondary mode rather than the default.
Table 8. Summary of DuoSign backend API endpoints.
MethodRoutePurpose
POST/api/translateRuns standard text-to-gloss translation and returns a single response payload.
POST/api/translate/fastReturns the rule-based translation path optimised for low latency.
POST/api/translate/streamStreams progressive translation updates over SSE for immediate UI feedback.
POST/api/translate/audioAccepts recorded audio and returns transcription/gloss output via Whisper integration.
GET/api/vocabularyReturns available gloss vocabulary metadata used by the frontend.
GET/api/pose/{gloss}Serves precomputed binary .pose landmark data for a given gloss token.
GET/api/video/{gloss}Serves the selected source sign video asset for a given gloss token.
POST/api/export/videoConverts recorded client media to downloadable MP4 (FFmpeg pipeline).
GET/api/healthExposes service health status for uptime checks and deployment monitoring.
